halfLife.notes: Very short half-life — rapid clearance. This means switching FROM agomelatine requires no washout from agomelatine's side; the drug clears within hours. Marked first-pass effect — bioavailability ~3% (range 1–80%); highly variable inter-individual exposure. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

activeMetabolite.notes: No clinically significant active metabolites.

cypInteractions.switchingRelevance: CRITICAL: Agomelatine is predominantly metabolised by CYP1A2. Strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin) increase agomelatine exposure up to 60-fold — fluvoxamine is CONTRAINDICATED with agomelatine. Moderate CYP1A2 inhibitors (estrogens, mexiletine) should also be avoided. Smoking (CYP1A2 inducer) markedly reduces exposure — smokers may need dose review. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

maoiWashout.notes: Agomelatine is not serotonergic but standard 14-day caution applies per Maudsley guidelines. FROM agomelatine to any antidepressant: no washout needed (t½ ~2h). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

discontinuationSyndromeRisk.notes: Very short half-life means no discontinuation syndrome on stopping. No dose taper required before stopping. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

agomelatine.formulationNotes: Start at 25 mg nocte. If no response after 2 weeks, increase to 50 mg nocte. Always take at night due to melatonergic mechanism. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.
specialConsiderations: MANDATORY LFT MONITORING: Hepatotoxicity risk (rare but serious). Check ALTs at baseline, 3, 6, 12 weeks, then periodically. Stop immediately if ALT >3× ULN.
CONTRAINDICATED with fluvoxamine (CYP1A2 inhibitor — 60× exposure increase).
Avoid in hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh A or above).
Smokers: CYP1A2 induction reduces levels — may need dose optimisation or drug may be less effective.
No serotonin syndrome risk — mechanism does not involve serotonin reuptake inhibition.
Night-time dosing only — activates MT1/MT2 melatonin receptors; daytime dosing defeats the mechanism.

amisulpride.formulationNotes: Biphasic D2/D3 pharmacology: low doses (50–300 mg/day) predominantly block presynaptic autoreceptors — may improve negative symptoms and depression. Higher doses (400–800 mg) provide full postsynaptic D2 blockade for positive symptoms. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.
specialConsiderations: Dose-dependent mechanism: low doses may worsen positive symptoms if used below therapeutic antipsychotic range — be explicit about the treatment goal when dosing.
QTc risk is moderate — ECG at baseline; more QTc prolongation than risperidone.
Very high prolactin elevation — similar to risperidone; monitor for hormonal side effects.
No CYP interactions — useful in complex polypharmacy.
Renal clearance — dose halving in moderate renal impairment (CrCl 10–30 mL/min).

aripiprazole.formulationNotes: Tablets only in MY. Akathisia is the most common dose-limiting AE — counsel patients to report restlessness early. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

activeMetabolite.name: Carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide
activeMetabolite.notes: Active and potentially toxic metabolite. Co-administration of valproate raises the epoxide level without raising the parent CBZ level — patients can develop toxicity at therapeutic CBZ levels when valproate is added. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

cypInteractions.switchingRelevance: Carbamazepine is a POWERFUL broad-spectrum enzyme inducer (CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A4, P-gp). It significantly reduces plasma levels of: antipsychotics (haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, clozapine), lamotrigine, valproate, hormonal contraceptives, warfarin, methadone, and many others. When STOPPING carbamazepine in a patient on other drugs, levels of those drugs RISE — dose reduction of the co-medication may be needed. When STARTING CBZ, levels FALL — doses may need increasing. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

reboundPsychosisRisk.notes: No rebound psychosis but stopping carbamazepine triggers a major drug interaction cascade: all co-prescribed drugs that were induced now rise to pre-CBZ levels. This is especially dangerous with clozapine (seizure threshold lowered) and antipsychotics. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

carbamazepine.formulationNotes: Controlled-release (Tegretol CR) preferred — reduces peak-trough fluctuation and lowers peak-related side effects (diplopia, dizziness, nausea). Switch between formulations is not always 1:1 in dose — may need monitoring. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.
specialConsiderations: HLA-B*1502 SCREENING MANDATORY IN ASIANS (DANGER): Steven-Johnson syndrome / TEN risk is dramatically higher (up to 10×) in HLA-B*1502-positive patients. This allele occurs in ~15% of Han Chinese, Thai, and Filipino populations — prevalent in Malaysian Chinese, Malay (some), and Iban. Screen ALL Asian patients with HLA-B*1502 before prescribing. Do NOT start if positive (consider alternative).
HLA-A*3101 in European populations (less relevant in Malaysia): associated with SJS/DRESS risk — screen if available.
Drug interactions (autoinduction): CBZ reduces its own levels over 1–4 weeks. Recheck levels after 4–6 weeks and adjust dose.
Contraceptive failure: carbamazepine reduces OCP efficacy. Warn patients — use barrier method in addition, or use non-hormonal IUD.
Monitoring: FBC, U&E, LFTs, and CBZ levels at baseline and 3-monthly. Target level 17–50 µmol/L (for mood). Agranulocytosis: rare but dangerous — any unexpected infection or bruising → urgent FBC.
Hyponatraemia: SIADH is a recognised side effect — check sodium in elderly patients or those on concurrent diuretics.
Withdrawal: taper SLOWLY (over ≥ 4 weeks). Stopping carbamazepine causes all induced co-medications to rise — monitor levels and clinical response carefully.
citations: HLA-B*1502 and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Chung et al. NEJM 2004.
Tegretol (carbamazepine) Summary of Product Characteristics. Novartis.

activeMetabolite.name: 7-hydroxychlorpromazine
activeMetabolite.notes: Multiple active metabolites contribute to prolonged and unpredictable pharmacokinetics. Accumulation possible with long-term use. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

cypInteractions.switchingRelevance: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors raise chlorpromazine levels and worsen EPS/sedation. Carbamazepine (CYP3A4 inducer) reduces levels. Fluvoxamine (CYP1A2 inhibitor) raises levels. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

chlorpromazine.formulationNotes: Tablets, syrup and IM injection available. Photosensitivity is a notable side effect — counsel patients about sun protection. Monitor QTc. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.
specialConsiderations: Phenothiazine class — highest QTc risk among FGAs; ECG mandatory at baseline and on dose escalation.
Significant anticholinergic burden — dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, cognitive impairment.
Photosensitivity — advise sun protection.
Jaundice (cholestatic hepatitis) — rare but serious; monitor LFTs.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome risk — common to all antipsychotics but particularly with FGAs.

activeMetabolite.name: Norclozapine (N-desmethylclozapine)
activeMetabolite.notes: Active metabolite contributes to overall pharmacology; norclozapine:clozapine ratio is sometimes interpreted alongside plasma level. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

cypInteractions.switchingRelevance: Smoking is a potent CYP1A2 inducer — sudden cessation can DOUBLE clozapine levels within 1-2 weeks. Counsel every patient on stable clozapine who plans to stop smoking. Strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin) are largely contraindicated. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

metabolicRisk.notes: Among the worst antipsychotics for weight gain, glucose dysregulation, dyslipidaemia. Mandatory metabolic monitoring at baseline, 3 months, 6 months, then annually. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

lai.notes: No long-acting injectable formulation.

reboundPsychosisRisk.notes: Clozapine withdrawal carries the highest relapse risk of any antipsychotic, including possible cholinergic rebound (clozapine has potent M1/M3 antagonism). NEVER stop abruptly unless agranulocytosis or myocarditis dictates. Re-challenge protocol applies after >48 hour interruption — restart at 12.5 mg. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

clozapine.formulationNotes: Tablets. Patient registration on the local clozapine monitoring service is mandatory before first prescription. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

activeMetabolite.notes: Desvenlafaxine IS the active metabolite of venlafaxine. No further active metabolites of clinical significance.

cypInteractions.switchingRelevance: Unlike venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine is not significantly metabolised by CYP2D6 — plasma levels are less variable across CYP2D6 phenotypes. Moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor — may raise levels of co-prescribed CYP2D6 substrates (risperidone, haloperidol). No washout advantage over venlafaxine for switching purposes. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

maoiWashout.notes: Same MAOI washout rules as venlafaxine — 14 days off desvenlafaxine before starting any MAOI; 14 days off any MAOI before starting desvenlafaxine. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

desvenlafaxine.formulationNotes: Extended-release tablets — do NOT crush, cut or chew. Swallow whole. 50 mg/day is the recommended effective dose for most patients; 100 mg/day offers no clear additional efficacy but higher side-effect burden. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.
specialConsiderations: Therapeutic equivalency to venlafaxine is not direct — dose conversion is approximate. Venlafaxine 75 mg ≈ desvenlafaxine 50 mg is a common reference.
CYP2D6 inhibition (moderate) — monitor risperidone, TCAs, opioids metabolised by CYP2D6.

haloperidol.formulationNotes: Tablets and IM injection (acute use). QTc check at baseline and on dose increases above 5 mg/day is prudent. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

halfLife.notes: Half-life is dramatically affected by co-medications. With valproate (UGT inhibitor): half-life ~70h — lamotrigine doses must be roughly HALVED. With carbamazepine/phenytoin/rifampicin (UGT inducers): half-life ~12–15h — lamotrigine doses must be roughly DOUBLED. Always check for enzyme inducers/inhibitors before prescribing. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

cypInteractions.switchingRelevance: Lamotrigine is a UGT substrate — not CYP. Critical interactions: Valproate INHIBITS LTG metabolism (double levels → halve dose). Carbamazepine/phenytoin/hormonal contraceptives INDUCE LTG metabolism (halve levels → double dose). Starting or stopping either of these drugs requires systematic LTG dose adjustment to avoid toxicity (SJS) or loss of efficacy. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

reboundPsychosisRisk.notes: No rebound psychosis. Abrupt discontinuation can precipitate breakthrough mood episodes or (in epilepsy) seizures. Taper over 2 weeks recommended. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

lamotrigine.formulationNotes: Dispersible tablets allow precise slow titration — important for SJS risk minimisation. Always titrate SLOWLY regardless of formulation. The specific titration rate depends entirely on whether valproate, carbamazepine, or neither is co-prescribed. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.
specialConsiderations: SLOW TITRATION MANDATORY (DANGER): Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) risk is dramatically increased by rapid dose escalation. The titration schedule depends on concurrent medications — follow the regime-specific schedule exactly.
Titration with valproate: start at 25 mg every OTHER day for 2 weeks, then 25 mg OD for 2 weeks, then increase in 25–50 mg steps every 1–2 weeks.
Titration without enzyme modifier: start at 25 mg OD for 2 weeks, then 50 mg OD for 2 weeks, then increase in 50 mg steps every 1–2 weeks.
Titration with CBZ/inducer: start at 50 mg OD for 2 weeks, then 100 mg OD (in divided doses) for 2 weeks, then increase in 100 mg steps every 1–2 weeks.
Rash warning: any rash in the first 8 weeks must be evaluated urgently — stop lamotrigine unless rash clearly unrelated to the drug.

Pregnancy: lowest teratogenic risk of the mood stabilizers — preferred choice in women who may become pregnant (risk not zero; neural tube defect risk small, no neurodevelopmental signal). High-dose folic acid pre-conception recommended.
Hormonal contraception interaction: combined OCP reduces lamotrigine levels by ~50%. Warn patients on OCP — may need dose adjustment. Pill-free week causes LTG level fluctuation.
citations: Lamictal (lamotrigine) Summary of Product Characteristics. GSK.

halfLife.notes: Half-life increases with age and in renal impairment. Renally cleared — dose proportional to GFR. Twice-daily dosing common in Malaysia; some evidence for single nocte dosing. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

activeMetabolite.notes: No active metabolite. Unchanged lithium ion is excreted by kidneys.

cypInteractions.switchingRelevance: Lithium has no CYP interactions — it is excreted renally unchanged. Key interactions: NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors raise lithium levels (reduce renal clearance). Diuretics (especially thiazides) markedly raise lithium levels. Dehydration and low sodium intake raise levels. Relevant in Ramadan (fasting, dehydration risk). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

reboundPsychosisRisk.notes: Abrupt lithium discontinuation can precipitate manic rebound — taper over at least 2–4 weeks if stopping. Discontinuation-induced mania may be more severe than pre-treatment episodes. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

lithium.formulationNotes: Controlled-release (Priadel) preferred for lower peak levels, less polyuria, and potentially better tolerability. Standard-release tablets allow more flexible dosing. Both are available in Malaysia. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.
specialConsiderations: Narrow therapeutic index: target serum level 0.6–1.0 mmol/L (maintenance), 0.8–1.0 mmol/L (acute mania). Check 12 h post-dose.
Mandatory baseline and monitoring: U&E, eGFR, TFT, Ca²⁺, weight, ECG in patients > 40 years.
Teratogenicity: Ebstein's anomaly risk (relative risk modest but counsel all women of reproductive age).
Toxicity: starts at > 1.5 mmol/L (coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea). Severe at > 2.0 mmol/L. Emergency: haemodialysis.
Dehydration risk: any illness causing sweating, diarrhoea or vomiting can cause toxicity — patients must be counselled to hold dose and seek review.
Ramadan: Fasting and dehydration risk — check levels more frequently during Ramadan. Consider twice-daily dosing at Suhoor + Iftar. Do NOT skip doses.

Strong CYP3A4 inducers (carbamazepine, rifampicin) reduce levels — may need dose increase. Avoid co-prescription with grapefruit juice. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

agomelatine-to-escitalopram.rationale: Agomelatine (MT1/MT2 agonist, 5-HT2C antagonist; t½ ~2h; no discontinuation syndrome; no serotonergic reuptake activity) to escitalopram (SSRI). The very short half-life of agomelatine means it clears within hours — no washout period is required from agomelatine's side. Agomelatine produces no serotonin reuptake inhibition, so there is no pharmacodynamic serotonin overlap concern when starting escitalopram. Practically: agomelatine can be stopped the same day escitalopram is started. A brief overlap is used here for clinical safety and to verify tolerability. Mandatory: Check LFTs before stopping agomelatine (hepatotoxicity monitoring exit check). Contraindication note: fluvoxamine is NOT escitalopram, but ensure no CYP1A2 inhibitor is inadvertently co-prescribed during any brief overlap. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start escitalopram 10 mg. Continue agomelatine 25 mg nocte. Check exit LFTs (ALT) — agomelatine hepatotoxicity monitoring final check. No serotonin overlap hazard: agomelatine has no serotonergic reuptake activity.
Review escitalopram tolerability (nausea, insomnia). Continue agomelatine — patient still taking nocte dose.
Stop agomelatine. Continue escitalopram 10 mg. No discontinuation syndrome expected from agomelatine (t½ ~2h). Titrate escitalopram to 20 mg after 4 weeks if inadequate response.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Agomelatine 25 mg ≈ escitalopram 10 mg (both standard effective doses for MDD). Not pharmacologically equivalent — different mechanisms. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

agomelatine-to-mirtazapine.rationale: Agomelatine (MT1/MT2 agonist; t½ ~2h; no discontinuation syndrome; melatonergic sleep mechanism) to mirtazapine (NaSSA: α2-antagonist, 5-HT2/3 antagonist, H1 antagonist; heavy sedation; significant weight gain). Both drugs help sleep — agomelatine via melatonin agonism, mirtazapine via H1 blockade and 5-HT2C antagonism. Switching may increase sedation significantly. No serotonergic overlap hazard. Exit LFT check before stopping agomelatine. Start mirtazapine at 15 mg nocte and consolidate before stopping agomelatine. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start mirtazapine 15 mg nocte. Continue agomelatine 25 mg nocte. Check exit LFTs. Counsel about increased sedation — mirtazapine sedation is more pronounced than agomelatine's. Take both at night. Warn about significant appetite increase and weight gain on mirtazapine.
Review mirtazapine tolerability (sedation, weight, mood). Continue agomelatine.

Stop agomelatine. Continue mirtazapine 15 mg nocte. No discontinuation syndrome from agomelatine. Titrate mirtazapine to 30 mg at 2 weeks if tolerated and response inadequate (counter-intuitively, 30 mg is less sedating than 15 mg due to additional noradrenergic activation).

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Agomelatine 25 mg → mirtazapine 15 mg (starting dose). Target mirtazapine 30–45 mg for full efficacy. Not pharmacologically equivalent — different mechanisms. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

agomelatine-to-sertraline.rationale: Agomelatine (MT1/MT2 agonist, 5-HT2C antagonist; t½ ~2h; no discontinuation syndrome; no serotonergic reuptake activity) to sertraline (SSRI). Agomelatine clears within hours — no washout needed. No pharmacodynamic serotonin overlap hazard. Agomelatine can be stopped the same day sertraline is started. A brief 7-day overlap is used for clinical comfort and LFT exit monitoring. Sertraline has a favourable interaction profile — no CYP1A2 inhibition concerns. Exit LFTs should be checked before stopping agomelatine. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start sertraline 50 mg. Continue agomelatine 25 mg nocte. Check exit LFTs (agomelatine final hepatotoxicity monitoring check). Sertraline: start at 50 mg, GI side effects common in first 1–2 weeks — take with food.
Review sertraline tolerability. Continue agomelatine.
Stop agomelatine. Continue sertraline 50 mg. No discontinuation syndrome from agomelatine. Titrate sertraline to 100 mg at 4 weeks if response inadequate.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Agomelatine 25 mg ≈ sertraline 50 mg (standard effective starting doses for MDD). Different mechanisms — not pharmacologically equivalent. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

agomelatine-to-venlafaxine.rationale: Agomelatine (MT1/MT2 agonist; t½ ~2h; no discontinuation syndrome; no serotonergic reuptake activity) to venlafaxine (SNRI). Agomelatine clears within hours — no washout needed. No pharmacodynamic serotonin overlap hazard since agomelatine does not inhibit serotonin reuptake. Start venlafaxine at low dose (37.5 mg or 75 mg XR) and titrate. Agomelatine can be stopped the same day venlafaxine is started. Brief overlap for clinical continuity. Exit LFT check before stopping agomelatine. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start venlafaxine XR 75 mg. Continue agomelatine 25 mg nocte. Check exit LFTs. Counsel patient: venlafaxine may cause nausea, sweating, headache in first 1–2 weeks. Take with food. Always use XR formulation where available.
Review venlafaxine tolerability. Continue agomelatine.
Stop agomelatine. Continue venlafaxine XR 75 mg. No discontinuation syndrome from agomelatine (t½ ~2h). Titrate venlafaxine to 150 mg at 4 weeks if response inadequate.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Agomelatine 25 mg ≈ venlafaxine 75 mg (standard starting effective doses). Not pharmacologically equivalent — different mechanisms. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

amisulpride-to-aripiprazole.rationale: Amisulpride (full D2 antagonist) to aripiprazole (partial D2/D3 agonist). Common reasons: prolactin elevation causing sexual dysfunction or amenorrhoea, QTc concerns, desire for weight-neutral drug, or akathisia unexpectedly better tolerated. Aripiprazole's partial D2 agonism carries a significant akathisia risk when switching from a full D2 antagonist — patients stabilised on high D2 blockade may find the relative dopaminergic activation distressing. This risk is highest in the first 2–4 weeks. Cross-taper preferred over direct switch to allow gradual receptor adaptation. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start aripiprazole 10 mg. Continue amisulpride 400 mg. Counsel patient about akathisia risk — restlessness, inability to sit still, worst in first 2 weeks. Propranolol or low-dose diazepam can be used if severe.
Increase aripiprazole to 15 mg (target). Plateau amisulpride. Akathisia peak risk period — review at end of week 1. QTc risk begins to reduce as aripiprazole does not prolong QTc.
Reduce amisulpride to 200 mg. Aripiprazole at target dose. Insomnia and activation may emerge as amisulpride's sedative effect diminishes.
Reduce amisulpride to 100 mg. Monitor for sleep onset difficulties. Melatonin or short-term promethazine can bridge sleep difficulties.
Stop amisulpride. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Prolactin normalises rapidly after amisulpride stops. Counsel female patients about possible menstrual cycle restoration.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Amisulpride 400 mg ≈ aripiprazole 15 mg (Leucht et al. CMD method, Schizophrenia Bulletin 2015). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

amisulpride-to-haloperidol.rationale: Both amisulpride and haloperidol are high-affinity D2 antagonists with similar receptor binding profiles, making this switch relatively smooth pharmacologically. Common reasons: need for IM/IV route (acute psychosis, non-compliance), formulary constraints, or cost. Both drugs elevate prolactin and carry EPS risk — the switch is essentially a lateral move within the high-D2-blockade class. Haloperidol carries a higher EPS risk than amisulpride, especially at higher doses — EPS and akathisia should be anticipated and managed. Both drugs carry QTc-prolongation risk (haloperidol especially at high IV doses or in combination). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start haloperidol 2 mg. Continue amisulpride 400 mg. ECG at baseline. Anticholinergic agent (e.g. procyclidine 5 mg PRN) should be prescribed for dystonia, especially in young males.
Increase haloperidol to 4 mg. Reduce amisulpride to 200 mg. Monitor for EPS — stiffness, tremor, akathisia. If EPS appears, consider reducing haloperidol rather than adding anticholinergic long-term.
Reduce amisulpride to 100 mg. Haloperidol at target. Check ECG — QTc with haloperidol.
Stop amisulpride. Continue haloperidol 4 mg. Repeat ECG at 4 weeks. Review EPS burden at each visit.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Amisulpride 400 mg ≈ haloperidol 4 mg (Maudsley 15th CPZ-equivalence table; note: haloperidol 2 mg ≈ CPZ 100 mg, amisulpride 200 mg ≈ CPZ 100 mg — so amisulpride 400 mg ≈ haloperidol 4 mg by proxy). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

amisulpride-to-lurasidone.rationale: Amisulpride (D2/D3 antagonist, QTc risk, renal excretion) to lurasidone (D2, 5-HT2A, 5-HT7 antagonist, partial 5-HT1A agonist, low QTc risk). Common reason: QTc concerns with amisulpride — lurasidone is one of the antipsychotics with the least QTc effect. Also: desire for antidepressant augmentation profile (5-HT7 and 5-HT1A activity), or metabolic improvement (lurasidone weight-neutral). Critical prescribing note: lurasidone must be taken with food (≥350 kcal) for adequate bioavailability — patient education at initiation is essential. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start lurasidone 40 mg with the main meal. Continue amisulpride 400 mg. Counsel explicitly: lurasidone must be taken with at least 350 kcal of food — subtherapeutic levels result from fasted dosing.
Increase lurasidone to 80 mg with main meal. Plateau amisulpride. QTc: the total QTc burden is reducing as lurasidone does not prolong QTc; amisulpride risk remains until it is stopped.
Reduce amisulpride to 200 mg. Lurasidone at standard therapeutic dose. Monitor renal function (amisulpride is renally excreted — dose-reduce amisulpride taper further if eGFR <30).
Reduce amisulpride to 100 mg. EPS: lurasidone carries moderate EPS risk — monitor for stiffness, akathisia.
Stop amisulpride. Continue lurasidone 80 mg with main meal. Repeat ECG at 4 weeks to confirm QTc normalisation after amisulpride cessation.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Amisulpride 400 mg ≈ lurasidone 80 mg (inferred from DDD-method equivalences: both ≈ olanzapine 10 mg by proxy; limited direct data for lurasidone). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

amisulpride-to-olanzapine.rationale: Amisulpride (selective D2/D3 antagonist, no anticholinergic or antihistamine activity) to olanzapine (multi-receptor antagonist: D2, 5-HT2A, H1, M1–M5, α1). Common reasons: insufficient response to amisulpride, prominent negative symptoms better targeted by olanzapine's 5-HT2A component, or QTc concerns with amisulpride. Cross-taper allows gradual receptor-profile transition. Amisulpride has no significant anticholinergic activity so withdrawal rebound is mild — the main risk is loss of D2 coverage during transition. Olanzapine's sedative onset is faster than its antipsychotic effect, so nocte dosing from day 1 aids sleep during switch. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start olanzapine 5 mg nocte alongside amisulpride 400 mg. Record baseline weight, fasting glucose, and fasting lipids before starting olanzapine.
Increase olanzapine to 10 mg nocte. Plateau amisulpride. Allow olanzapine to approach steady state before tapering amisulpride.
Reduce amisulpride to 200 mg. Olanzapine at target dose. No cholinergic rebound expected from amisulpride reduction (no anticholinergic activity).
Reduce amisulpride to 100 mg. Monitor QTc normalisation — amisulpride QTc risk diminishes as dose falls.
Stop amisulpride. Continue olanzapine 10 mg. Schedule metabolic review at 4 and 12 weeks. Weight likely to increase — dietary counselling advisable.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Amisulpride 400 mg ≈ olanzapine 10 mg (Leucht et al. CMD method, Schizophrenia Bulletin 2015; Maudsley 15th dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

amisulpride-to-quetiapine.rationale: Amisulpride (D2/D3) to quetiapine (D2, 5-HT2A, H1, M1, α1/α2). Common reasons: QTc concerns with amisulpride, desire for antidepressant augmentation effect (norquetiapine), prominent insomnia, or reduction in prolactin. Quetiapine's substantial anticholinergic and antihistaminergic burden will increase sedation during overlap — especially relevant if the patient drives or works with machinery. Both drugs carry moderate QTc risk; the overlap period requires ECG monitoring. Quetiapine initiation should begin nocte. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start quetiapine 100 mg nocte. Continue amisulpride 400 mg. Warn about additive sedation. ECG at baseline for QTc monitoring. Postural hypotension common on quetiapine initiation — advise patient to rise slowly.
Increase quetiapine to 200 mg nocte. Plateau amisulpride. Check ECG for combined QTc if electrolyte abnormality suspected.
Increase quetiapine to 400 mg (or split 200 mg BD if daytime sedation is excessive). Reduce amisulpride to 200 mg.
Reduce amisulpride to 100 mg. Quetiapine approaching full clinical effect. Prolactin likely normalising as amisulpride tapers.
Stop amisulpride. Continue quetiapine 400 mg. Repeat ECG at 4–6 weeks. Metabolic monitoring if weight gain or pre-diabetes risk factors present.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Amisulpride 400 mg ≈ quetiapine 400 mg (Leucht et al. CMD method, Schizophrenia Bulletin 2015). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

amisulpride-to-risperidone.rationale: Both amisulpride and risperidone are high D2 affinity antagonists with significant prolactin elevation. Common reasons for switching: cost or formulary, tolerability of QTc with amisulpride, or seeking risperidone LAI continuation. Receptor profiles are broadly similar — D2/D3 plus 5-HT2A (risperidone) — so clinical discontinuity during taper is low. Both elevate prolactin; the overlap period carries additive hyperprolactinaemia risk. ECG required: both prolong QTc. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start risperidone 2 mg. Continue amisulpride 400 mg. ECG at baseline — both drugs prolong QTc; check combined QTc at week 2.
Increase risperidone to 4 mg. Plateau amisulpride. Check serum electrolytes (K+, Mg2+) — hypokalaemia amplifies QTc risk of both drugs.
Reduce amisulpride to 200 mg. Risperidone at target. Note: prolactin elevation is additive during overlap — if symptomatic, expedite amisulpride withdrawal.
Reduce amisulpride to 100 mg. QTc risk falling as amisulpride dose decreases.
Stop amisulpride. Continue risperidone 4 mg. Repeat ECG at 4–6 weeks post-switch. If LAI transition planned, initiate risperidone LAI protocol.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Amisulpride 400 mg ≈ risperidone 4 mg (Leucht et al. CMD method, Schizophrenia Bulletin 2015). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

aripiprazole-lai-to-aripiprazole.rationale: Switching from Abilify Maintena (400 mg IM monthly) to oral aripiprazole. The depot has a long t½ (~30–46 days at steady state) and continues releasing for weeks after the last injection. Start oral aripiprazole at the target maintenance dose; the depot provides a natural taper. No bridging with oral during the depot tail is pharmacologically necessary but monitored exposure may be elevated early on. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Skip the next scheduled Maintena injection. Start oral aripiprazole 10 mg. Depot continues releasing — combined levels will be above single-drug target initially. Counsel patient.
Increase oral aripiprazole to 15 mg. Depot level falling but still substantial. Monitor for akathisia (most common aripiprazole ADR).
Depot level approximately halved from peak. Oral 15 mg now primary dose. Assess tolerability and response.
Depot substantially cleared (~2 months). Oral aripiprazole 15 mg as effective monotherapy.
Depot cleared (~3 months post-last-injection). Oral aripiprazole monotherapy confirmed. Adjust to 10–30 mg based on response.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Abilify Maintena 400 mg/month ≈ oral aripiprazole 15 mg/day (Maudsley 15th approximate equivalency). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

safetyFlags.title: Akathisia
safetyFlags.body: Akathisia is the most common neurological adverse reaction with aripiprazole. Titrate oral dose gradually and counsel patient before initiation.

safetyFlags.title: Extended depot tail
safetyFlags.body: Abilify Maintena t½ is ~30–46 days at steady state. Plasma levels persist for ~3 months after the final injection. Start oral at conservative dose to avoid excessive combined exposure.

aripiprazole-lai-to-paliperidone-lai.rationale: SGA-to-SGA depot switch, typically driven by inadequate psychotic symptom control on aripiprazole (partial agonism insufficient in some patients) or persistent akathisia. Paliperidone palmitate's two-dose deltoid loading protocol (150 mg day 1, 100 mg day 8) achieves therapeutic levels rapidly. Aripiprazole LAI's very long effective half-life (~30-46 days) means that after the last injection, meaningful aripiprazole levels persist for 2-3 months, providing ongoing D2 cover throughout the PP-LAI loading and early maintenance period. No additional oral overlap is needed. The partial agonism of aripiprazole will diminish as paliperidone (full antagonist) competes for D2 receptors — akathisia and activation symptoms should resolve during this phase. Prolactin will rise as aripiprazole (low prolactin) is replaced by paliperidone (high prolactin) — counsel accordingly. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Give Invega Sustenna 150 mg deltoid (loading dose 1) in place of next scheduled Maintena injection. Do NOT give Maintena today. Aripiprazole depot tail provides sustained D2 cover. Counsel patient that akathisia should resolve over coming weeks.
Invega Sustenna 100 mg deltoid (loading dose 2, day 8 ± 2 days). Aripiprazole depot still present. PP-LAI reaching therapeutic range.

First maintenance Sustenna 100 mg (deltoid or gluteal). Aripiprazole substantially cleared. Assess prolactin (will have risen), EPS (should be low with PP), and symptom control. Monthly Sustenna thereafter.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: aripiprazole LAI 400 mg/4 weeks ≈ paliperidone palmitate 100 mg/4 weeks (Maudsley 15th, LAI equivalence). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

aripiprazole-to-amisulpride.rationale: Aripiprazole (partial D2/D3 agonist, very long half-life ~75 h plus dehydroaripiprazole ~94 h) to amisulpride (full D2 antagonist). Common reasons: insufficient positive symptom control on aripiprazole, need for more sedation, or intolerable akathisia from aripiprazole. Because aripiprazole's half-life is extremely long, effective plasma levels persist for 3–5 weeks after the last dose. This means that amisulpride can be started at full therapeutic dose from day 1 — aripiprazole's residual partial agonism provides a natural buffer against abrupt coverage loss. The cross-taper can be shorter than usual for this reason. ECG required: amisulpride prolongs QTc; baseline before starting. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start amisulpride 400 mg at full therapeutic dose. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Aripiprazole's very long half-life (active drug persists 3–5 weeks after stopping) means full D2 coverage is maintained throughout. Baseline ECG for amisulpride.
Plateau both drugs. Amisulpride approaching steady state. QTc: check baseline ECG if not done. Aripiprazole plasma levels are still present despite any dose reduction.
Reduce aripiprazole to 10 mg. Amisulpride well established. Expect resolution of aripiprazole-associated akathisia or insomnia if these were the reason for switching.
Reduce aripiprazole to 5 mg. Effective aripiprazole levels remain clinically significant due to the long half-life even at this low dose.
Stop aripiprazole. Continue amisulpride 400 mg. Note: residual aripiprazole will continue to wash out for several further weeks — EPS and QTc picture stabilises gradually. Repeat ECG at 6 weeks.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Aripiprazole 15 mg ≈ amisulpride 400 mg (Leucht et al. CMD method, Schizophrenia Bulletin 2015). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

aripiprazole-to-aripiprazole-lai.rationale: Standard oral-to-LAI conversion for patients established on oral aripiprazole who would benefit from the adherence and relapse-prevention advantages of a monthly depot. The Abilify Maintena protocol requires a mandatory 14-day oral aripiprazole overlap after the first injection because the depot microspheres take approximately 2 weeks to reach therapeutic serum levels from the injection site. Stopping oral aripiprazole before day 14 risks a sub-therapeutic window. Tolerability should have been confirmed on oral aripiprazole first. The first injection is given at the patient's usual oral dose equivalent. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Administer Abilify Maintena 400 mg IM (gluteal or deltoid). Continue oral aripiprazole 15 mg daily — 14-day oral overlap is MANDATORY. Counsel patient that the injection takes 2 weeks to become active.
Continue oral aripiprazole 15 mg. Depot releasing but not yet at therapeutic concentration. No dose changes.
STOP oral aripiprazole today (14-day overlap complete). Depot now therapeutic. Second injection not due until day 28-29.
Second monthly Maintena 400 mg injection. Oral aripiprazole is stopped. Ongoing: one injection every 28 days. If strong CYP2D6 or CYP3A4 inhibitors are co-prescribed, reduce dose to 300 mg.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Oral aripiprazole 15 mg/day → Abilify Maintena 400 mg monthly. For oral doses of 10–20 mg, 400 mg monthly is standard. For 30 mg oral, consider 400 mg with close monitoring. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

aripiprazole-to-haloperidol.rationale: SGA-to-FGA switch from aripiprazole. Pharmacologically notable: aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist, while haloperidol is a full D2 antagonist. As haloperidol builds and displaces aripiprazole at D2 receptors, the activation and energy effects of aripiprazole will diminish — this is usually welcome in patients with aripiprazole-induced agitation or akathisia. The reverse transition (akathisia improving) should be monitored. Aripiprazole's very long half-life (~75h) means it provides a natural slow washout. Baseline ECG mandatory for haloperidol. Metabolic parameters: aripiprazole is metabolically neutral; haloperidol is also low metabolic risk — no significant change expected. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start haloperidol 2 mg. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Baseline ECG mandatory. Akathisia from aripiprazole should begin to resolve as full D2 antagonism increases.
Increase haloperidol to 5 mg target. Plateau aripiprazole — its long half-life means taper can be gentle.
Begin reducing aripiprazole to 10 mg. Haloperidol at steady state. Assess for haloperidol-induced EPS — have benzhexol available.
Reduce aripiprazole to 5 mg. Haloperidol dominant. Aripiprazole still present due to long half-life — minimal rebound expected.
Stop aripiprazole. Continue haloperidol 5 mg. Recheck QTc at haloperidol steady state. Monitor for haloperidol EPS burden.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: aripiprazole 15 mg ≈ haloperidol 5 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

aripiprazole-to-lurasidone.rationale: Aripiprazole (partial D2/D3 agonist, very long half-life ~75 h) to lurasidone (full D2 antagonist, short-moderate half-life ~18 h). Both are metabolically neutral and low-QTc-risk SGAs. Common reasons: intolerable akathisia on aripiprazole, insufficient positive symptom control, or simplifying food-independent dosing replaced by food-dependent dosing (a trade-off). Lurasidone must be taken with ≥350 kcal — a critical patient education point. Aripiprazole's very long half-life means effective levels persist well after stopping — this provides a natural buffer during the transition. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start lurasidone 40 mg with main meal. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Counsel patient: lurasidone must be taken with ≥350 kcal of food every day for adequate absorption.
Increase lurasidone to 80 mg with main meal. Reduce aripiprazole to 10 mg. Akathisia should begin to resolve as aripiprazole dose reduces.
Reduce aripiprazole to 5 mg. Aripiprazole's long half-life means residual partial D2 agonism is still present — smooth transition.
Stop aripiprazole. Continue lurasidone 80 mg with main meal. Residual aripiprazole will continue to wash out over 3–4 weeks after stopping — monitor for any akathisia recurrence.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Aripiprazole 15 mg ≈ lurasidone 80 mg (inferred from DDD equivalence; both ≈ olanzapine 10 mg by proxy). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

aripiprazole-to-olanzapine.rationale: Typically driven by akathisia, significant anxiety or insomnia on aripiprazole where sedation is a therapeutic goal, or by inadequate psychotic symptom control. Olanzapine's sedation, anticholinergic and antihistaminergic properties provide faster symptomatic relief than quetiapine for agitation. Cross-taper: start olanzapine nocte at half-target while aripiprazole is still running (its long half-life buffers any coverage gap), then taper aripiprazole once olanzapine reaches target. Counsel the patient clearly about the metabolic risk escalation — olanzapine has among the highest weight gain and glycaemic risk of all SGAs. Establish baseline weight, fasting glucose and lipids before initiating. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start olanzapine 5 mg nocte. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Sedation and improved sleep expected from night 1. Warn about metabolic monitoring requirement.
Increase olanzapine to 10 mg nocte (target dose). Plateau aripiprazole for one more week — allow olanzapine to stabilise.
Begin tapering aripiprazole to 10 mg. Olanzapine at steady state. Akathisia should have resolved.
Reduce aripiprazole to 5 mg. Aripiprazole's long half-life means residual D2 partial agonism is still present — gradual washout continues.
Stop aripiprazole. Continue olanzapine 10 mg. Confirm metabolic baseline is documented. Schedule weight check at 4 and 12 weeks.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: aripiprazole 15 mg ≈ olanzapine 10 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

aripiprazole-to-quetiapine.rationale: Most commonly driven by akathisia, anxiety or insomnia on aripiprazole — quetiapine provides immediate sedative and anxiolytic relief via H1 and α1 blockade even at 50 mg, before antipsychotic-range doses are reached. Aripiprazole's very long half-life (~75h oral; even longer LAI) means it provides a natural slow taper — it does not need to be abruptly stopped. Cross-taper: introduce quetiapine nocte while aripiprazole is still on board, then reduce aripiprazole once quetiapine has reached near-target. Counsel the patient about the metabolic shift — moving to higher metabolic burden with quetiapine. QTc monitoring recommended — quetiapine has moderate QTc risk. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start quetiapine 50 mg nocte. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Immediate sedation benefit expected — advise driving caution. Patient should notice sleep improvement within days.
Increase quetiapine to 100 mg. Plateau aripiprazole — allow quetiapine to build before tapering. Akathisia from aripiprazole should be reducing.
Increase quetiapine to 200 mg. Begin reducing aripiprazole to 10 mg. Aripiprazole's long half-life provides a gradual washout.
Quetiapine at 300 mg target. Reduce aripiprazole to 5 mg. Confirm akathisia has resolved.
Stop aripiprazole. Continue quetiapine 300 mg. Baseline weight and fasting glucose — metabolic monitoring begins here.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: aripiprazole 15 mg ≈ quetiapine 300 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

aripiprazole-to-risperidone.rationale: Most often driven by inadequate psychotic symptom control on aripiprazole (partial agonism insufficient for positive symptoms in some patients), or by akathisia where a full D2 antagonist provides better symptom suppression. Cross-taper: introduce risperidone at low dose while aripiprazole is still running, then taper aripiprazole once risperidone is at therapeutic range. Aripiprazole's long half-life means it washes out gradually — abrupt cessation is not needed and not preferred. Counsel about the pharmacological shift: moving to full D2 antagonism will increase prolactin and raise (not lower) EPS risk. Prolactin monitoring at 3 months is prudent. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start risperidone 1 mg. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Overlap is safe — aripiprazole's partial agonism and risperidone's full antagonism co-exist without problematic pharmacodynamic clash at low risperidone doses.
Increase risperidone to 2 mg. Plateau aripiprazole — allow risperidone to build before tapering.
Increase risperidone to 3 mg. Begin reducing aripiprazole to 10 mg. EPS monitoring begins — risperidone EPS risk increases above 4 mg.
Risperidone at 4 mg target. Reduce aripiprazole to 5 mg. Aripiprazole washout in progress — residual partial agonism diminishing.
Stop aripiprazole. Continue risperidone 4 mg. Check prolactin at 3 months if clinically relevant. Monitor EPS above 4 mg.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: aripiprazole 15 mg ≈ risperidone 4 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

carbamazepine-to-lamotrigine.rationale: This switch has a critical pharmacokinetic hazard: carbamazepine is a potent UGT inducer, so the patient will already be on a higher-than-normal lamotrigine dose to achieve therapeutic levels (CBZ roughly halves lamotrigine levels). As CBZ is tapered and withdrawn, the UGT induction is lost and lamotrigine levels will RISE — potentially into the toxic range (SJS risk). Lamotrigine dose MUST be reduced in step with the CBZ taper. The target lamotrigine maintenance dose on monotherapy will be roughly HALF the co-prescribed dose. This is a high-stakes pharmacokinetic interaction requiring close monitoring and lamotrigine level checking. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start lamotrigine at 100 mg/day (given CBZ induction, this is an appropriate starting dose — NOT the usual 25 mg slow-titration start). Continue carbamazepine 400 mg/day unchanged. Monitor for rash.
Increase lamotrigine to 150 mg/day. Hold CBZ. Check for rash and lamotrigine tolerability.
Increase lamotrigine to 200 mg/day (target monotherapy maintenance dose). Begin CBZ taper at next step.
Reduce CBZ to 200 mg/day. Reduce lamotrigine to 175 mg — compensating for rising LTG levels as CBZ induction falls. Check LTG level if available.
Reduce CBZ to 100 mg/day. Reduce lamotrigine to 125 mg.
Stop carbamazepine. Lamotrigine monotherapy target 100 mg/day. Titrate up or down based on response and tolerability. Check lamotrigine level 2 weeks after CBZ is stopped.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Not a dose-equivalency switch. Lamotrigine target dose for mood disorder is 100–200 mg/day as monotherapy. The 200 mg initial target compensates for CBZ induction; the dose is reduced to ~100 mg as CBZ is withdrawn. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

citations: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines 14th Edition — Lamotrigine drug interactions
Anderson GD. Pharmacokinetic drug interactions with carbamazepine. Clin Pharmacokinet. 1998.
contraindications: HLA-B*1502-positive patients (SJS risk with both carbamazepine and lamotrigine — screen before initiating either drug in Asian patients)
Any unexplained rash on current carbamazepine

carbamazepine-to-lithium.rationale: Carbamazepine to lithium: Indicated when greater mania prevention is needed, or for CBZ intolerance/failure. KEY HAZARDS: (1) Carbamazepine enzyme reversal — CBZ is a potent CYP inducer; as it is tapered, induction of CYP3A4/2C9/2B6 reverses over 2–4 weeks, causing rising plasma levels of all co-medications that are CYP substrates (note: lithium has NO CYP metabolism — it is renally cleared, so this hazard affects other concurrent medications, not lithium itself). (2) Neurotoxicity during overlap — both CBZ and lithium can cause CNS toxicity; even at therapeutic levels, the combination can cause additive effects (ataxia, confusion, tremor). Monitor carefully during overlap phase. (3) Lithium narrow therapeutic index — titrate to serum levels, not weight. Start lithium while CBZ is still present; do not reduce CBZ until lithium is established at therapeutic level. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start lithium 400 mg/day. Continue carbamazepine 800 mg/day. Baseline renal function, TFT, U&E, ECG. Check lithium level at day 5. Counsel patient about double CNS effect during overlap — may experience more drowsiness, tremor. Warn about sick-day rules for lithium.
Increase lithium to 800 mg/day if level below target and well tolerated. Hold carbamazepine. Check lithium level at day 12.

Increase lithium to 1000 mg/day if level <0.6 mmol/L (12 h post-dose). Begin CBZ taper: reduce carbamazepine to 600 mg/day. As CBZ reduces, CYP enzyme induction reverses — check any co-medications that may have rising levels (e.g. antidepressants, antipsychotics, oral contraceptives).
Reduce carbamazepine to 600 mg/day. Lithium level check — ensure therapeutic. CBZ enzyme reversal ongoing — monitor co-medication toxicity.
Reduce carbamazepine to 400 mg/day. Lithium is primary mood stabiliser. Enzyme induction largely reversed by this stage.
Reduce carbamazepine to 200 mg/day. Final step before stopping. Recheck lithium level — confirm 0.6–1.0 mmol/L.

Stop carbamazepine. Continue lithium (dose adjusted to level). Recheck lithium level 2–4 weeks after CBZ stopped to confirm no change (lithium has no CYP interactions so level should be stable). Also review levels of any other medications previously affected by CBZ induction — now enzyme reversal is complete, levels will be elevated.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Not dose-equivalent. Lithium target defined by serum level (0.6–1.0 mmol/L maintenance; 12 h post-dose). Note: lithium does not interact pharmacokinetically with carbamazepine (no CYP involvement for lithium). Neurotoxicity during overlap is a pharmacodynamic interaction. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

contraindications: Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min) — lithium contraindicated.

carbamazepine-to-valproate.rationale: Carbamazepine to valproate: Indicated for treatment failure on CBZ, teratogenicity risk minimisation (valproate is higher teratogenic risk — discuss carefully), or intolerance. KEY PHARMACOKINETIC HAZARD: Carbamazepine is a potent CYP inducer. As CBZ is tapered and withdrawn, induction of CYP3A4/2C9 is progressively reversed — this causes rising plasma levels of any co-medications that are CYP3A4/2C9 substrates (enzyme reversal). Valproate itself is partially CYP2C9-metabolised, so valproate levels may RISE as CBZ is withdrawn — monitor closely and be prepared to reduce valproate dose if toxicity emerges. Also: VPA inhibits CBZ-epoxide hydrolase during overlap, increasing CBZ-epoxide toxicity (see valproate-to-carbamazepine for full discussion). Start valproate low and titrate before CBZ is substantially reduced. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start valproate 500 mg/day. Continue carbamazepine 800 mg/day. CBZ induction active — valproate levels will be lower than expected during co-prescription phase. Check baseline LFTs, FBC. EURAP/teratogenicity counselling documented for women of reproductive age if initiating valproate.
Increase valproate to 1000 mg/day. Hold carbamazepine. Monitor for CBZ-epoxide toxicity symptoms (double vision, ataxia, dizziness) — VPA inhibits epoxide hydrolase, raising CBZ-E levels.

Increase valproate to 1500 mg/day (target). Begin CBZ taper: reduce carbamazepine to 600 mg/day. As CBZ reduces, enzyme induction reverses and valproate levels will begin to rise — watch for VPA side effects (sedation, tremor).
Reduce carbamazepine to 400 mg/day. Check valproate level — levels likely rising as CBZ induction reverses. May need to reduce valproate dose if side effects or high level.
Reduce carbamazepine to 200 mg/day. Confirm valproate level. Carbamazepine enzyme reversal almost complete — VPA level may have risen significantly. Adjust VPA dose to level.
Reduce carbamazepine to 100 mg/day. Final step. Recheck valproate level — enzyme induction fully reversed by this stage.

Stop carbamazepine. Continue valproate (dose adjusted to level, typically 50–100 mg/L). Recheck valproate level 2–4 weeks after CBZ stopped to confirm stability. Carbamazepine enzyme-inducing effects persist for up to 4 weeks after stopping — continue close level monitoring.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Not dose-equivalent. Valproate dose during CBZ co-prescription phase will appear sub-therapeutic due to enzyme induction — do not over-increase. Target monotherapy valproate 1000–2000 mg/day (level 50–100 mg/L). Re-establish level 4 weeks after CBZ fully withdrawn. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

contraindications: Current pregnancy or planning pregnancy — valproate is highly teratogenic. Switch only if no safer alternative and full risk minimisation in place.

chlorpromazine-to-aripiprazole.rationale: Chlorpromazine (heavily anticholinergic, antihistaminergic, sedating FGA) to aripiprazole (partial D2/D3 agonist, no anticholinergic/antihistamine activity). This is one of the most challenging antipsychotic transitions due to the extreme receptor profile contrast. Aripiprazole has NONE of the H1, M1, or α1 blockade of CPZ, so there is NO mitigation of cholinergic rebound on CPZ withdrawal. Insomnia, akathisia, and GI rebound are expected to be significant. Additionally, aripiprazole's partial D2 agonism causes akathisia particularly in patients previously on full D2 blockade. Proceed very slowly — 6 weeks minimum. Strong patient counselling required. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start aripiprazole 5 mg. Continue chlorpromazine 400 mg. Counsel patient explicitly about two major side effects to anticipate: (1) akathisia from aripiprazole — report restlessness early; (2) insomnia and nausea as CPZ is reduced — monitor and manage proactively. Propranolol PRN for akathisia.
Increase aripiprazole to 10 mg. Plateau chlorpromazine. Review akathisia — if severe, do not increase aripiprazole further this week.
Increase aripiprazole to 15 mg (target). Reduce chlorpromazine to 300 mg. Cholinergic rebound begins — aripiprazole provides no anticholinergic buffer.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 200 mg. Insomnia will worsen as H1 blockade falls — melatonin or promethazine PRN. Manage akathisia if present.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 100 mg. Sedation substantially reduced. Monitor activation, anxiety, and sleep.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 50 mg. Most of the clinical transition is now complete.
Stop chlorpromazine. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Prolactin normalises — counsel female patients about menstrual restoration. QTc will improve. Review metabolic parameters.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Chlorpromazine 400 mg ≈ aripiprazole 15 mg (CPZ-equivalence: 100 mg CPZ ≈ 3.75 mg aripiprazole per Maudsley 15th dose equivalence). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

chlorpromazine-to-olanzapine.rationale: Chlorpromazine (high anticholinergic, antihistaminergic, antiadrenergic, QTc-prolonging FGA) to olanzapine (SGA with similar sedative and anticholinergic profile but better EPS and lower seizure-threshold risk). This FGA→SGA transition is driven by EPS, tardive dyskinesia risk, or seeking a more targeted receptor profile. Chlorpromazine has one of the highest anticholinergic burdens of any antipsychotic — abrupt withdrawal causes severe cholinergic rebound. The cross-taper must be SLOW (4–6 weeks minimum). Olanzapine's receptor profile overlaps chlorpromazine's H1 and muscarinic burden, so the cholinergic rebound from CPZ withdrawal may be partially mitigated by olanzapine. Monitor for unmasking of tardive dyskinesia as CPZ is reduced. Seizure threshold: CPZ lowers it significantly; olanzapine less so — consider EEG if history of seizures. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start olanzapine 5 mg nocte. Continue chlorpromazine 400 mg. Record baseline weight, fasting glucose, fasting lipids. ECG at baseline — chlorpromazine prolongs QTc.
Increase olanzapine to 10 mg nocte (target). Plateau chlorpromazine. Allow olanzapine to establish clinical effect before tapering the heavily anticholinergic CPZ.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 300 mg. Cholinergic rebound risk begins — nausea, sweating, GI upset possible. Go slowly; return to 400 mg for one week if symptoms are distressing.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 200 mg. Monitor for signs of unmasking of tardive dyskinesia as FGA dose falls. Review postural hypotension — CPZ's α1 blockade is subsiding.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 100 mg. QTc improving as CPZ dose reduces. Continue to monitor for cholinergic rebound.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 50 mg. Final taper step.
Stop chlorpromazine. Continue olanzapine 10 mg. Repeat ECG at 4–6 weeks. Tardive dyskinesia review — document any dyskinetic movements. Metabolic monitoring at 4 and 12 weeks.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Chlorpromazine 400 mg ≈ olanzapine 10 mg (CPZ-equivalence: 100 mg CPZ ≈ 2.5 mg olanzapine; Maudsley 15th dose equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

chlorpromazine-to-quetiapine.rationale: Chlorpromazine to quetiapine — both drugs share H1, M1, and α1 receptor activity, so the transition is pharmacologically smoother than CPZ to a cleaner SGA (e.g. risperidone). Quetiapine's receptor profile partially overlaps CPZ, which mitigates cholinergic rebound during taper. Both drugs also prolong QTc and carry metabolic risk. The main advantages of quetiapine over CPZ are improved EPS profile, reduced seizure-threshold lowering, and the availability of XR formulation for once-daily dosing. Quetiapine initiation nocte recommended for sedation management. Cross-taper over 4–6 weeks due to CPZ's heavy receptor burden. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start quetiapine 100 mg nocte. Continue chlorpromazine 400 mg. Baseline ECG (both drugs prolong QTc). Record baseline metabolic parameters.
Increase quetiapine to 200 mg nocte. Plateau chlorpromazine. Both drugs additive for sedation — caution with driving.
Increase quetiapine to 400 mg (target; can split 200 mg BD if daytime sedation excessive). Reduce chlorpromazine to 300 mg.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 200 mg. Quetiapine's H1 and M1 activity partially attenuates CPZ cholinergic rebound — but still monitor for nausea and insomnia.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 100 mg. QTc: combined QTc risk reducing as CPZ dose falls.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 50 mg.
Stop chlorpromazine. Continue quetiapine 400 mg. Repeat ECG at 4–6 weeks. Metabolic monitoring at 4 and 12 weeks.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Chlorpromazine 400 mg ≈ quetiapine 400 mg (CPZ-equivalence: 100 mg CPZ ≈ 75–100 mg quetiapine per Maudsley 15th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

chlorpromazine-to-risperidone.rationale: Chlorpromazine (high anticholinergic/antihistaminergic FGA) to risperidone (low anticholinergic SGA). The reduction in anticholinergic burden is significant — risperidone has minimal muscarinic activity. This means cholinergic rebound from CPZ withdrawal is NOT attenuated by risperidone (unlike the CPZ→olanzapine or CPZ→quetiapine switch). Cholinergic rebound symptoms must be anticipated and managed explicitly. The QTc risk from CPZ will decrease but risperidone also has moderate QTc prolongation. EPS profile moves from low-potency FGA (more sedating, less EPS) to moderate-potency SGA (more EPS than olanzapine/quetiapine). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start risperidone 1 mg. Continue chlorpromazine 400 mg. ECG at baseline. Warn about cholinergic rebound as CPZ is tapered — risperidone does not attenuate muscarinic rebound.
Increase risperidone to 2 mg. Plateau chlorpromazine. Allow risperidone to establish before tapering CPZ.
Increase risperidone to 4 mg (target). Reduce chlorpromazine to 300 mg. Cholinergic rebound likely — nausea, insomnia, diaphoresis.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 200 mg. Monitor QTc — additive risk during overlap though reducing as CPZ dose falls.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 100 mg. Prolactin rising on risperidone — monitor for sexual side effects.
Reduce chlorpromazine to 50 mg. EPS review — risperidone has more EPS burden than CPZ at these doses.
Stop chlorpromazine. Continue risperidone 4 mg. Repeat ECG at 4–6 weeks. Review EPS and prolactin.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Chlorpromazine 400 mg ≈ risperidone 4 mg (CPZ-equivalence: 100 mg CPZ ≈ 1 mg risperidone per Maudsley 15th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

desvenlafaxine-to-escitalopram.rationale: Desvenlafaxine (SNRI; t½ ~11h; high discontinuation syndrome risk) to escitalopram (SSRI; t½ ~27h; moderate discontinuation syndrome risk). Switch from SNRI to SSRI — reducing noradrenergic activity, often for blood pressure or sweating. Escitalopram is not a CYP2D6 inhibitor — no interaction with desvenlafaxine during cross-taper. Both are serotonergic — low serotonin syndrome risk at standard doses. Desvenlafaxine must be tapered carefully to avoid discontinuation syndrome. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start escitalopram 10 mg. Continue desvenlafaxine 50 mg. Both drugs present: combined serotonergic load at standard doses is clinically acceptable.
Continue both at same doses. Assess tolerability. If excessive serotonergic symptoms (agitation, tremor, tachycardia) reduce desvenlafaxine earlier.

Stop desvenlafaxine. Continue escitalopram 10 mg. Desvenlafaxine discontinuation syndrome possible at this step — if symptoms emerge, slower taper may be needed. Titrate escitalopram to 20 mg at 4 weeks if response inadequate.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Desvenlafaxine 50 mg → escitalopram 10 mg (standard effective doses). Not pharmacologically equivalent — different mechanisms. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

desvenlafaxine-to-mirtazapine.rationale: Desvenlafaxine (SNRI; t½ ~11h; high discontinuation syndrome risk) to mirtazapine (NaSSA; t½ ~20–40h; H1 sedation; weight gain). Switch reasons: inadequate response, sexual dysfunction, desire for sedation/sleep improvement. Mirtazapine's α2-antagonism blocks presynaptic noradrenaline autoreceptors — combined with desvenlafaxine's noradrenaline reuptake inhibition during cross-taper, additive noradrenergic stimulation is possible (agitation, tachycardia — monitor). H1 blockade from mirtazapine provides sedation but may be excessive initially. Taper desvenlafaxine carefully. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start mirtazapine 15 mg nocte. Continue desvenlafaxine 50 mg. Combined noradrenergic effect during cross-taper: monitor for agitation, tremor, sweating. Counsel about sedation from mirtazapine and expected weight gain.
Continue both at current doses. Assess tolerability. Consider desvenlafaxine dose reduction if noradrenergic side effects excessive.
Stop desvenlafaxine. Continue mirtazapine 15 mg nocte. Monitor for desvenlafaxine discontinuation syndrome at stop. Titrate mirtazapine to 30 mg at 2 weeks if response inadequate.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Desvenlafaxine 50 mg → mirtazapine 15 mg (start dose; titrate to 30–45 mg). Not pharmacologically equivalent. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

desvenlafaxine-to-sertraline.rationale: Desvenlafaxine (SNRI; t½ ~11h; high discontinuation syndrome risk) to sertraline (SSRI; t½ ~26h; moderate CYP2D6 inhibition). Sertraline is a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor — desvenlafaxine is not primarily CYP2D6-metabolised (unlike venlafaxine) so this interaction is less significant. Both serotonergic — standard low risk cross-taper at therapeutic doses. Taper desvenlafaxine carefully; sertraline can be started at full dose from day 1. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start sertraline 50 mg. Continue desvenlafaxine 50 mg. Both serotonergic — combined load is clinically acceptable at standard doses. Counsel: GI side effects from sertraline in first 1–2 weeks are common.
Review sertraline tolerability. Continue desvenlafaxine. Optional: reduce desvenlafaxine to 25 mg (half tablet, off-label) at this step for more graded taper.
Stop desvenlafaxine. Continue sertraline 50 mg. Titrate sertraline to 100 mg at 4 weeks if inadequate response.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Desvenlafaxine 50 mg → sertraline 50 mg (standard starting doses). Not pharmacologically equivalent. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

desvenlafaxine-to-venlafaxine.rationale: Desvenlafaxine to venlafaxine: Desvenlafaxine IS the active metabolite of venlafaxine (O-desmethylvenlafaxine). This is essentially a formulation/prodrug switch within the same pharmacological class. The pharmacokinetic overlap is favourable — both drugs act on the same targets (SERT + NET). Discontinuation syndrome risk is high for both. Approach: start venlafaxine at approximate equivalent dose, then taper desvenlafaxine. Dose conversion: desvenlafaxine 50 mg ≈ venlafaxine 75 mg (approximate; individual variation expected). Both carry high discontinuation syndrome risk — never stop either abruptly. The switch should be smooth given the pharmacological similarity. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start venlafaxine XR 75 mg. Continue desvenlafaxine 50 mg. Pharmacologically very similar switch — smooth transition expected. No serotonin syndrome risk of clinical concern at these doses.
Assess tolerability on dual SNRI. If excess side effects (tachycardia, sweating, nausea), reduce desvenlafaxine sooner.

Stop desvenlafaxine. Continue venlafaxine XR 75 mg. If stopping desvenlafaxine causes discontinuation symptoms, use a slower taper (50 mg → 25 mg for 1 week → stop). Titrate venlafaxine to 150 mg at 4 weeks if response inadequate.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Desvenlafaxine 50 mg ≈ venlafaxine 75 mg (approximate conversion; desvenlafaxine 50 mg ≈ venlafaxine 75 mg is a commonly used reference). Individual variation expected. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

duloxetine-to-sertraline.rationale: SNRI-to-SSRI swap, often when noradrenergic adverse effects predominate or response was insufficient. Duloxetine's high discontinuation-syndrome risk requires a graded reduction; sertraline is started low and titrated. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start sertraline 25 mg. Hold duloxetine 60 mg.
Halve duloxetine to 30 mg. Increase sertraline to 50 mg. Watch for discontinuation symptoms.
Hold duloxetine. Increase sertraline to 100 mg target.
Stop duloxetine. Continue sertraline 100 mg. Slow this final step if disc symptoms emerge.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: duloxetine 60 mg ≈ sertraline 100 mg (Maudsley 14th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

duloxetine-to-venlafaxine.rationale: SNRI-to-SNRI swap, considered for inefficacy or when venlafaxine's higher-dose noradrenergic activity is desired. Both drugs carry significant discontinuation-syndrome risk; cross-taper minimises withdrawal on the duloxetine side. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start venlafaxine XR 37.5 mg. Hold duloxetine 60 mg. Check baseline blood pressure.
Halve duloxetine to 30 mg. Increase venlafaxine to 75 mg XR.
Hold duloxetine. Increase venlafaxine to 150 mg XR target. Re-check blood pressure.
Stop duloxetine. Continue venlafaxine 150 mg XR. Slow this final step if disc symptoms emerge.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: duloxetine 60 mg ≈ venlafaxine 150 mg XR (Maudsley 14th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

escitalopram-to-agomelatine.rationale: Escitalopram (SSRI; t½ ~27h; moderate discontinuation syndrome risk) to agomelatine (MT1/MT2 agonist, 5-HT2C antagonist; t½ ~2h; no serotonergic reuptake activity). Switch reasons: sexual dysfunction, weight gain, inadequate response on SSRI, desire for sleep-targeting antidepressant. Escitalopram has moderate discontinuation syndrome risk — taper gradually over at least 2 weeks. Agomelatine can be started during the escitalopram taper without serotonin syndrome risk (agomelatine does not inhibit serotonin reuptake). CRITICAL: LFTs must be checked BEFORE starting agomelatine (hepatotoxicity monitoring baseline). Agomelatine is contraindicated in hepatic impairment. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start agomelatine 25 mg nocte. Continue escitalopram 20 mg. CHECK BASELINE LFTs (ALT) BEFORE starting agomelatine — mandatory hepatotoxicity monitoring. If ALT >3× ULN do not start agomelatine. No serotonin overlap concern — agomelatine has no serotonergic reuptake activity.
Reduce escitalopram to 10 mg. Continue agomelatine 25 mg. Monitor for discontinuation symptoms (dizziness, 'brain zaps', mood change) — mild at this step.

Stop escitalopram. Continue agomelatine 25 mg nocte. Some patients may experience brief discontinuation symptoms on final escitalopram stop — usually mild and self-limiting with escitalopram. Titrate agomelatine to 50 mg at 2 weeks if response inadequate.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Escitalopram 20 mg → agomelatine 25 mg (standard doses for MDD). Not pharmacologically equivalent — different mechanisms. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

contraindications: Hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh A or above) — agomelatine contraindicated.
ALT >3× ULN at baseline — do not start agomelatine.

escitalopram-to-desvenlafaxine.rationale: Escitalopram (SSRI; t½ ~27h) to desvenlafaxine (SNRI; t½ ~11h). Switch from SSRI to SNRI — adding noradrenergic component for treatment-resistant depression, fatigue, or pain. Escitalopram is not a CYP2D6 inhibitor — no interaction with desvenlafaxine. Both serotonergic — standard low-risk cross-taper at therapeutic doses. Start desvenlafaxine at 50 mg during the cross-taper then taper escitalopram. Desvenlafaxine has predictable pharmacokinetics due to minimal CYP2D6 metabolism. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start desvenlafaxine 50 mg. Continue escitalopram 20 mg. No significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Combined serotonergic load at standard doses is clinically acceptable. Counsel about potential early nausea, sweating from desvenlafaxine.
Reduce escitalopram to 10 mg. Continue desvenlafaxine 50 mg. Monitor for discontinuation symptoms from escitalopram reduction.
Stop escitalopram. Continue desvenlafaxine 50 mg. Titrate to 100 mg at 4 weeks if response inadequate (limited additional efficacy for most patients but some benefit).

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Escitalopram 20 mg → desvenlafaxine 50 mg (standard effective doses). Not pharmacologically equivalent. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

escitalopram-to-fluoxetine.rationale: Switch to fluoxetine when a longer-half-life SSRI is preferred (poor adherence, planned tapering down the line, breastfeeding considerations). Brief overlap is sufficient given fluoxetine's slow wash-in. Escitalopram is reduced as fluoxetine begins to accumulate. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start fluoxetine 20 mg. Hold escitalopram 10 mg.
Halve escitalopram to 5 mg. Hold fluoxetine.
Stop escitalopram. Continue fluoxetine 20 mg. Counsel patient about future 5-week MAOI washout obligation.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: escitalopram 10 mg ≈ fluoxetine 20 mg (Maudsley 14th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

escitalopram-to-sertraline.rationale: Common first-line SSRI swap when escitalopram is ineffective or poorly tolerated. Both drugs have clean PK profiles; a brief cross-taper is sufficient. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start sertraline 25 mg in the morning. Hold escitalopram 10 mg.
Halve escitalopram to 5 mg. Increase sertraline to 50 mg.
Stop escitalopram. Continue sertraline 100 mg target.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: escitalopram 10 mg ≈ sertraline 100 mg (Maudsley 14th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

escitalopram-to-venlafaxine.rationale: SSRI-to-SNRI swap when serotonergic-only treatment is insufficient and noradrenergic activity is desired. Brief cross-taper because escitalopram disc risk is moderate and venlafaxine titrates slowly anyway. Check baseline blood pressure before introducing venlafaxine. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start venlafaxine XR 37.5 mg. Hold escitalopram 10 mg. Check baseline blood pressure.
Halve escitalopram to 5 mg. Increase venlafaxine to 75 mg XR.
Hold escitalopram. Increase venlafaxine to 150 mg XR target. Re-check blood pressure.
Stop escitalopram. Continue venlafaxine XR 150 mg. Counsel re venlafaxine's very-high disc risk if later stopped.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: escitalopram 10 mg ≈ venlafaxine 150 mg XR (Maudsley 14th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

escitalopram-to-vortioxetine.rationale: Escitalopram (SSRI; t½ ~27h; moderate discontinuation syndrome risk) to vortioxetine (SMS; multimodal serotonergic; t½ ~66h). Reasons: cognitive impairment on escitalopram, sexual dysfunction, or partial response with desire for multimodal augmentation. Both are serotonergic — low but non-zero serotonin syndrome risk during brief overlap at standard doses. Escitalopram is not a CYP2D6 inhibitor — no dose adjustment needed for vortioxetine. Direct switch strategy: stop escitalopram and start vortioxetine on the same day. A very brief taper of escitalopram is included to reduce discontinuation syndrome risk. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start vortioxetine 10 mg. Reduce escitalopram to 10 mg (halving before stopping reduces discontinuation syndrome). Both at reduced dose for 7 days. Escitalopram is not a CYP2D6 inhibitor — no vortioxetine dose adjustment needed.
Stop escitalopram. Continue vortioxetine 10 mg. Monitor for escitalopram discontinuation symptoms (usually mild at this point). Titrate vortioxetine to 20 mg at 2–4 weeks if response inadequate.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Escitalopram 20 mg → vortioxetine 10 mg (standard effective starting doses). Not pharmacologically equivalent. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

fluoxetine-to-escitalopram.rationale: Switch from fluoxetine to escitalopram for tolerability or response reasons. Brief overlap is sufficient because norfluoxetine continues to circulate for 1-2 weeks after fluoxetine is discontinued, providing serotonergic bridge while escitalopram titrates up. Start escitalopram low to avoid additive load. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start escitalopram 5 mg. Hold fluoxetine 20 mg.
Stop fluoxetine. Norfluoxetine continues for 1-2 weeks — explain the invisible bridge to the patient.
Increase escitalopram to 10 mg target.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: fluoxetine 20 mg ≈ escitalopram 10 mg (Maudsley 14th). Slow escitalopram titration is intentional given norfluoxetine carry-over. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

fluoxetine-to-sertraline.rationale: Switching off fluoxetine because of inefficacy or side effects. The cross-taper is deliberately short because norfluoxetine continues to circulate for 1-2 weeks after fluoxetine is stopped, providing a built-in pharmacological bridge. Sertraline is started low and titrated slowly to avoid additive serotonergic load while norfluoxetine clears. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start sertraline 25 mg in the morning. Hold fluoxetine 20 mg.
Stop fluoxetine. Norfluoxetine will continue for 1-2 weeks — counsel patient that the ‘bridge’ is invisible but real.
Increase sertraline to 50 mg. Watch for serotonergic excess (tremor, hyperreflexia).
Increase sertraline to 100 mg target.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: fluoxetine 20 mg ≈ sertraline 100 mg (Maudsley 14th). Norfluoxetine carry-over justifies the slower upward sertraline titration. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

flupenthixol-lai-to-flupenthixol.rationale: Switching from flupenthixol decanoate (Fluanxol Depot) to oral flupenthixol (Fluanxol tablets). Flupenthixol decanoate has a t½ of ~17 days and continues releasing for 4–6 weeks after the last injection. Start oral flupenthixol when the next depot injection would have been due. Approximate dose equivalence: flupenthixol decanoate 40 mg/2 weeks ≈ oral flupenthixol 10–15 mg/day (Maudsley). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Skip the next scheduled depot injection. Start oral flupenthixol 6 mg/day. Depot continues releasing — monitor combined effect and EPS.
Depot level falling. Increase oral flupenthixol to 9 mg/day. Monitor EPS, prolactin, and mood.
Depot substantially cleared (~4 weeks). Oral flupenthixol 12 mg/day becoming sole therapeutic agent.
Depot cleared. Oral flupenthixol monotherapy established. Typical range 3–18 mg/day; adjust to lowest effective dose.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Flupenthixol decanoate 40 mg every 2 weeks ≈ oral flupenthixol 12 mg/day (approximate; Maudsley 15th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

safetyFlags.title: EPS risk (FGA)
safetyFlags.body: Flupenthixol is an FGA with significant EPS risk. Ensure anticholinergic prophylaxis is available if not already prescribed.

safetyFlags.title: Decanoate tail
safetyFlags.body: Flupenthixol decanoate t½ ~17 days. Therapeutic levels persist 4–6 weeks after the last injection. Start oral dose conservatively.

fluphenazine-lai-to-fluphenazine.rationale: Switching from fluphenazine decanoate (Modecate depot) to oral fluphenazine. Fluphenazine decanoate has a t½ of ~14 days and continues releasing for ~4–6 weeks after the last injection. Start oral fluphenazine when the next depot injection would have been due. Approximate equivalence: fluphenazine decanoate 25 mg/2 weeks ≈ oral fluphenazine 10 mg/day (rough estimate — consult Maudsley for specific dose pairs). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Skip next depot injection. Start oral fluphenazine 5 mg/day. Depot continues releasing. Monitor EPS carefully — fluphenazine is a high-potency FGA.
Depot level falling. Oral fluphenazine 5 mg/day. Monitor for akathisia, parkinsonism. Anticholinergic cover likely needed.
Depot substantially cleared (~4 weeks). Increase oral fluphenazine to 10 mg/day as primary agent.
Depot cleared. Oral fluphenazine monotherapy. Typical range 2.5–20 mg/day; titrate to lowest effective dose.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Fluphenazine decanoate 25 mg/2 weeks ≈ oral fluphenazine 10 mg/day (approximate; Maudsley 15th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

safetyFlags.title: EPS risk (high-potency FGA)
safetyFlags.body: Fluphenazine is a high-potency FGA. EPS (akathisia, acute dystonia, parkinsonism) are common. Anticholinergic prophylaxis strongly recommended.

safetyFlags.title: Tardive dyskinesia risk
safetyFlags.body: Long-term FGA use (and depot specifically) carries TD risk. Assess AIMS at baseline when switching to oral.

safetyFlags.title: Decanoate tail
safetyFlags.body: Fluphenazine decanoate t½ ~14 days. Therapeutic levels persist ~4–6 weeks after the last injection.

haloperidol-lai-to-aripiprazole-lai.rationale: FGA-to-SGA depot conversion targeting metabolic neutrality and QTc improvement. Aripiprazole LAI (Abilify Maintena) requires a mandatory 14-day oral aripiprazole overlap after the first injection because depot microspheres take ~2 weeks to reach therapeutic levels. The haloperidol decanoate depot tail (effective half-life ~21 days) provides D2 cover during both the oral overlap phase and beyond — there is no coverage gap. Risk of akathisia: aripiprazole's D2 partial agonism can precipitate akathisia when acting on a D2 receptor pool fully saturated by haloperidol. Counsel the patient early; if akathisia emerges consider propranolol 40 mg twice daily or a temporary low-dose benzodiazepine. QTc will improve as haloperidol clears. EPS, tardive movements and prolactin should normalise progressively over 3 months. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Skip next Haldol decanoate injection. Administer Abilify Maintena 400 mg IM (gluteal or deltoid). START oral aripiprazole 10 mg daily — 14-day overlap is MANDATORY. Haloperidol depot tail still providing D2 cover. Counsel patient about akathisia risk and to report inner restlessness early.

STOP oral aripiprazole today (14-day overlap complete). Abilify Maintena now therapeutic. Haloperidol depot clearing. Monitor akathisia — risk peaks in this phase as haloperidol full-antagonism recedes and aripiprazole partial agonism takes hold.
Second Maintena 400 mg injection. Haloperidol substantially cleared. Review akathisia, EPS, QTc and prolactin. Monthly Maintena thereafter.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: haloperidol decanoate 100 mg/4 weeks ≈ aripiprazole LAI 400 mg/4 weeks (Maudsley 15th, LAI equivalence). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

haloperidol-lai-to-haloperidol.rationale: Switching from haloperidol decanoate (long-acting depot) to oral haloperidol. Haloperidol decanoate has a t½ of ~21 days (range 14–35 days) and continues releasing for 6–8 weeks after the last injection. Start oral haloperidol when the next depot injection would have been due; the decanoate provides a natural taper. The oral/depot dose equivalence is approximately 1:10–15 (mg daily oral : mg decanoate per 4 weeks). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Skip the next scheduled decanoate injection. Start oral haloperidol 2 mg/day. Decanoate continues releasing — monitor for combined effect, particularly EPS.
Decanoate level declining. Increase oral haloperidol to 5 mg/day. Monitor EPS (akathisia, parkinsonism) and clinical state.
Decanoate substantially cleared (~6 weeks). Oral haloperidol 5 mg/day approaching sole therapeutic agent.
Decanoate cleared (~2 months). Oral haloperidol 5 mg/day monotherapy. Adjust 2–10 mg based on clinical response. Consider anticholinergic cover for EPS.
