doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Haloperidol decanoate 50 mg/month ≈ oral haloperidol 5 mg/day (Maudsley 15th; ratio ~1:10). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

safetyFlags.title: EPS risk (FGA)
safetyFlags.body: Haloperidol is a high-potency FGA with significant EPS risk. Ensure anticholinergic prophylaxis is available. Monitor for akathisia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia.

safetyFlags.title: ECG / QTc
safetyFlags.body: Haloperidol prolongs QTc. Obtain baseline ECG and monitor, especially at higher doses.

safetyFlags.title: Decanoate tail
safetyFlags.body: Haloperidol decanoate t½ ~21 days. Therapeutic levels persist 6–8 weeks after the last injection. Start oral dose conservatively.

haloperidol-lai-to-paliperidone-lai.rationale: The most clinically common FGA depot-to-SGA depot conversion — escaping haloperidol decanoate's EPS, tardive dyskinesia risk, hyperprolactinaemia and QTc burden while maintaining the adherence benefits of depot administration. Paliperidone palmitate's two-dose deltoid loading protocol (150 mg day 1, 100 mg day 8) reaches therapeutic levels quickly without needing a separate oral overlap. The haloperidol decanoate depot tail (half-life ~21 days; full clearance ~10 weeks) provides ongoing D2 cover during the PP-LAI loading period — combined exposure is clinically acceptable and preferred over a bare switch. Skip the next scheduled decanoate injection and commence PP-LAI loading. Monitor QTc: haloperidol's high QTc contribution will diminish over weeks as the depot clears. EPS, prolactin and tardive symptoms should be reviewed at 3 months when haloperidol has substantially cleared. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Skip next Haldol decanoate injection. Give Invega Sustenna 150 mg deltoid (loading dose 1). Haloperidol depot tail continues releasing — good D2 cover maintained. Counsel patient on expected improvement in EPS over coming months.
Invega Sustenna 100 mg deltoid (loading dose 2, day 8 ± 2 days). Haloperidol depot still present. PP-LAI levels building toward therapeutic range. QTc beginning to improve as haloperidol clears.
First maintenance Sustenna injection (100 mg; deltoid or gluteal). Haloperidol decanoate substantially cleared. Assess EPS, tardive movements, prolactin. Monthly Sustenna thereafter.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: haloperidol decanoate 100 mg/4 weeks ≈ paliperidone palmitate 100 mg/4 weeks (Maudsley 15th, LAI equivalence). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

haloperidol-lai-to-risperidone-lai.rationale: Common FGA-to-atypical depot conversion to escape EPS, hyperprolactinaemia or QTc concern. Skip the next scheduled Haldol decanoate; start Consta with oral risperidone overlap because Consta does not release for ~3 weeks. Haldol decanoate continues releasing for several weeks, providing concurrent D2 cover during the Consta loading gap. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Skip next Haldol decanoate. Inject Consta 25 mg deltoid. Start oral risperidone 2 mg/day for 21 days (cover during Consta release lag).
Second Consta 25 mg injection. Continue oral risperidone 2 mg. Haldol depot tail still significant.
Stop oral risperidone — Consta now clinically effective. Haldol depot fading.
Third Consta 25 mg injection. Haldol depot continues to clear.
Haldol substantially cleared. Maintenance Consta every 2 weeks.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: Haldol decanoate 100 mg/4 weeks ≈ Consta 25 mg/2 weeks (Maudsley 14th, conservative). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

haloperidol-to-amisulpride.rationale: Haloperidol (potent D2 antagonist, high EPS, low sedation) to amisulpride (D2/D3 selective, moderate EPS, low sedation, QTc risk). Both are high-D2-blockade drugs with similar clinical receptor profiles. Common reasons: high EPS burden on haloperidol (amisulpride generally has lower EPS at standard doses), desire to avoid depot initiation, cost, or need to switch to a drug without the known QTc risk of haloperidol at higher IV doses. EPS should improve on amisulpride. Both prolong QTc — ECG during overlap is important. Both elevate prolactin. Cross-taper can proceed at a standard pace as there is no significant anticholinergic component to manage. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start amisulpride 200 mg. Continue haloperidol 4 mg. Baseline ECG. Check renal function for amisulpride. EPS should begin to improve as amisulpride is introduced.
Increase amisulpride to 400 mg (target). Reduce haloperidol to 2 mg. QTc monitor — check ECG at week 2 if combined risk factors.
Reduce haloperidol to 1 mg. Amisulpride well established. Review EPS — if significantly improved, continue taper at this pace.

Stop haloperidol. Continue amisulpride 400 mg. Repeat ECG at 4–6 weeks. Review prolactin if patient previously symptomatic — amisulpride also elevates prolactin but may be less symptomatic than haloperidol.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Haloperidol 4 mg ≈ amisulpride 400 mg (Maudsley 15th CPZ-equivalence table: haloperidol 2 mg ≈ CPZ 100 mg, amisulpride 200 mg ≈ CPZ 100 mg). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

haloperidol-to-aripiprazole.rationale: FGA-to-SGA switch with metabolic neutrality as the primary goal. Plateau cross-taper is essential here: aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist and its activation of a fully antagonised (haloperidol-saturated) D2 receptor pool can precipitate akathisia early in the switch. The plateau phase allows aripiprazole to reach target dose and the D2 receptor pool to begin adapting before haloperidol is withdrawn. Do NOT rush the haloperidol taper. Akathisia is the main risk — counsel the patient to report inner restlessness, and differentiate from psychotic agitation. QTc will improve as high-risk haloperidol is replaced by low-risk aripiprazole. Prolactin will normalise progressively. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start aripiprazole 5 mg in the morning. Continue haloperidol 5 mg. Counsel patient about potential akathisia — advise to report restlessness early.
Increase aripiprazole to 10 mg. Hold haloperidol at 5 mg (plateau). Watch for akathisia — more likely in this early co-administration phase.
Increase aripiprazole to 15 mg target. Maintain haloperidol plateau for one more week — D2 receptor stabilisation in progress.
Begin tapering haloperidol to 2 mg. Aripiprazole at full target. QTc improving. Review anticholinergic agents — EPS driver reducing.
Reduce haloperidol to 1 mg. Prolactin normalisation underway. Stop anticholinergic if still prescribed.
Stop haloperidol. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Recheck QTc post-haloperidol clearance. Confirm akathisia has resolved.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: haloperidol 5 mg ≈ aripiprazole 15 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

haloperidol-to-haloperidol-lai.rationale: Standard oral-to-depot haloperidol conversion. The standard initiation dose of haloperidol decanoate is approximately 10–15× the daily oral dose (capped at 100 mg per first injection). A 28-day oral haloperidol overlap is required because the depot absorbs slowly from the oil vehicle for the first 4 weeks. Stopping oral haloperidol before day 28 risks a sub-therapeutic window. Oral dose is tapered to 50% after the first depot injection and stopped at day 28 as the depot releases to therapeutic levels. QTc must be monitored — haloperidol is a high QTc risk agent. If EPS worsens during the transition, anticholinergic agents (benzhexol) should be continued or started. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Give first Haldol Decanoate injection (50 mg deep gluteal IM). Continue oral haloperidol 5 mg/day. Counsel patient: depot takes 4 weeks to fully release — oral cover is essential during this period.
Continue oral haloperidol 5 mg. Depot still in absorption phase. Continue anticholinergic cover if prescribed.
Reduce oral haloperidol to 2 mg (half dose). Depot now releasing meaningfully. EPS assessment — anticholinergic review.
Stop oral haloperidol. Depot now at therapeutic release. Second injection due today (50 mg every 4 weeks for maintenance). Recheck QTc post-stabilisation.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate conversion: oral haloperidol 5 mg/day → haloperidol decanoate 50 mg/4 weeks (10× daily dose rule). For higher oral doses: 10 mg/day → 100 mg/4 weeks. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

haloperidol-to-lurasidone.rationale: Haloperidol (high-potency FGA; high EPS; moderate QTc; high prolactin) to lurasidone (SGA; low EPS; very low QTc; moderate prolactin; food-dependent). Common reasons: EPS burden (parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia risk with long-term haloperidol, akathisia), QTc concerns, or upgrading to an SGA with better tolerability. EPS should improve substantially on lurasidone. Prolactin falls moderately. QTc improves. CRITICAL counselling: lurasidone must be taken with ≥350 kcal of food — fasted dosing produces subtherapeutic levels. Haloperidol has low anticholinergic activity so cross-taper can proceed at a moderate pace without significant cholinergic rebound. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start lurasidone 40 mg with main meal. Continue haloperidol 4 mg. Counsel: lurasidone must be taken with ≥350 kcal every day. EPS improvement expected as lurasidone is introduced.
Increase lurasidone to 80 mg. Reduce haloperidol to 2 mg. QTc: check ECG — haloperidol QTc risk diminishes as dose falls.
Reduce haloperidol to 1 mg. EPS burden should be substantially reduced by this point.
Stop haloperidol. Continue lurasidone 80 mg with main meal. Repeat ECG at 4 weeks. Review EPS status — consider whether anticholinergic agents can now be withdrawn.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Haloperidol 4 mg ≈ lurasidone 80 mg (inferred from DDD equivalence; both ≈ olanzapine 10 mg by proxy). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

haloperidol-to-olanzapine.rationale: FGA-to-SGA switch, typically driven by EPS burden (parkinsonism, akathisia, tardive risk) or as part of a long-term treatment quality-of-life improvement. Introduce olanzapine first at half-target and stabilise before reducing haloperidol. Olanzapine's strong anticholinergic and antihistaminergic properties will provide cholinergic cover during the transition, reducing the risk of cholinergic rebound from haloperidol cessation. Warning: metabolic monitoring (weight, glucose, lipids) is mandatory — olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden among SGAs. If the patient is on an anticholinergic agent (e.g. benzhexol) for EPS, review the need to continue once haloperidol is stopped. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start olanzapine 5 mg nocte. Continue haloperidol 5 mg. Advise patient that EPS should improve over the coming weeks. Initial sedation from olanzapine expected.
Increase olanzapine to 10 mg nocte (target dose). Hold haloperidol at 5 mg for one more week to allow olanzapine to stabilise.
Reduce haloperidol to 2 mg. Olanzapine now providing primary antipsychotic cover. Review continuing anticholinergic agents — may no longer be needed.
Reduce haloperidol to 1 mg. EPS should be substantially improved. Review QTc — haloperidol's QTc contribution is reducing.
Stop haloperidol. Continue olanzapine 10 mg. Establish baseline metabolic markers if not done at initiation. Withdraw anticholinergic agent if still prescribed.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: haloperidol 5 mg ≈ olanzapine 10 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

haloperidol-to-paliperidone-lai.rationale: A common FGA-to-SGA depot switch — switching from oral haloperidol (high EPS, high QTc, no metabolic burden) to paliperidone palmitate LAI (lower EPS, moderate metabolic burden, same high prolactin burden). Paliperidone palmitate's two-dose deltoid loading protocol (150 mg day 1, 100 mg day 8) achieves therapeutic concentrations immediately — no oral paliperidone run-in is required. Oral haloperidol is continued alongside the PP loading to prevent a coverage gap, then tapered once PP reaches steady state at approximately 3–4 weeks. EPS will improve on switching from haloperidol to paliperidone, but not eliminate entirely — maintain anticholinergic agents until the transition is stable. QTc: haloperidol has high QTc risk; paliperidone LAI has low QTc risk — the switch itself reduces cardiac risk, but monitor QTc during the taper overlap as both are present briefly. Prolactin remains elevated — both haloperidol and paliperidone are high-prolactin agents. Metabolic monitoring from baseline as paliperidone carries moderate metabolic burden where haloperidol is near-zero. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Give Invega Sustenna 150 mg deltoid IM (loading dose 1). Continue oral haloperidol 5 mg. Counsel patient: 2 loading injections required at day 1 and day 8; maintenance monthly thereafter. Continue anticholinergic cover if prescribed. Baseline QTc.

Invega Sustenna 100 mg deltoid IM (loading dose 2, day 8 ± 2 days). Continue oral haloperidol 5 mg. PP-LAI building toward therapeutic range. Brief period of haloperidol + paliperidone overlap — QTc monitoring if cardiac risk factors present.
PP-LAI now therapeutic. Taper oral haloperidol to 2 mg. EPS may ease as haloperidol reduces — anticholinergic review. Metabolic baseline: weight, glucose.
Stop oral haloperidol. First maintenance Sustenna injection (100 mg; deltoid or gluteal). Monthly thereafter. QTc recheck: should improve with haloperidol cessation. Prolactin check at 3 months.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: haloperidol 5 mg/day ≈ paliperidone palmitate 100 mg/4 weeks (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table + LAI conversion). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

haloperidol-to-quetiapine.rationale: FGA-to-SGA switch where sedation, sleep benefit or mood stabilisation is a therapeutic goal alongside antipsychotic efficacy. Quetiapine's strong H1 and α1-adrenergic antagonism provides immediate sleep and anxiolytic benefits even at the starting 50 mg dose. Cross-taper: introduce quetiapine in the evening (nocte) while maintaining haloperidol, then taper haloperidol as quetiapine builds to antipsychotic-range doses (≥200 mg). Note QTc: both haloperidol (high) and quetiapine (moderate) prolong QTc — check baseline ECG and consider repeating at the point of maximum combined dose exposure (around day 7–14). Sedation will be more pronounced during the overlap phase; advise driving caution. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start quetiapine 50 mg nocte. Continue haloperidol 5 mg. Advise patient about sedation — best taken at bedtime. ECG at baseline if not recently done.
Increase quetiapine to 100 mg nocte. Plateau haloperidol. Consider repeat ECG — dual QTc burden peaks around this phase.
Increase quetiapine to 200 mg (divided or nocte). Reduce haloperidol to 2 mg. EPS improvement should be apparent.
Quetiapine at 300 mg target. Reduce haloperidol to 1 mg. Anticholinergic agent review — likely can be stopped as EPS driver withdraws.
Stop haloperidol. Continue quetiapine 300 mg. Repeat QTc — haloperidol's contribution has cleared. Metabolic monitoring: baseline weight and fasting glucose.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: haloperidol 5 mg ≈ quetiapine 300 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

haloperidol-to-risperidone.rationale: The most common FGA-to-SGA switch in Malaysian clinical practice — moving away from haloperidol's high EPS and tardive dyskinesia risk. Cross-taper: introduce risperidone first and build to therapeutic dose while tapering haloperidol gradually. Both drugs carry high prolactin liability, so prolactin-related side effects (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction) may persist. EPS monitoring remains important — risperidone carries moderate EPS risk, particularly above 4 mg/day. If the patient is on anticholinergic cover (benzhexol), review once haloperidol is stopped; haloperidol's higher EPS drive will no longer be present. QTc should normalise as haloperidol (high QTc risk) is withdrawn. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start risperidone 1 mg. Continue haloperidol 5 mg. Baseline QTc if not recently done — haloperidol QTc risk exits as risperidone enters.
Increase risperidone to 2 mg. Plateau haloperidol — allow risperidone to build before tapering.
Increase risperidone to 3 mg. Reduce haloperidol to 2 mg. EPS should begin to improve as haloperidol burden reduces.
Risperidone at 4 mg target. Reduce haloperidol to 1 mg. Review anticholinergic agent — may no longer be needed.
Stop haloperidol. Continue risperidone 4 mg. Stop anticholinergic if still prescribed. Recheck QTc — haloperidol's QTc contribution has cleared.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: haloperidol 5 mg ≈ risperidone 4 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

lamotrigine-to-carbamazepine.rationale: Lamotrigine to carbamazepine: Indicated for rapid cycling bipolar disorder or treatment failure on lamotrigine. KEY PHARMACOKINETIC HAZARDS: (1) Carbamazepine INDUCES lamotrigine metabolism (UGT induction) — as CBZ is titrated up, lamotrigine levels will FALL progressively. This means the apparent efficacy of lamotrigine will reduce as CBZ is added; do not interpret mood symptoms as carbamazepine failure — the lamotrigine dose may need increasing to compensate, or the lamotrigine taper can be accelerated. (2) CBZ autoinduction — carbamazepine induces its own metabolism over 4–6 weeks; initial CBZ levels will be higher than steady-state. (3) HLA-B*1502 screen before starting carbamazepine in South/South-East Asian patients (Malaysian population — SJS risk substantially higher). Lamotrigine also carries SJS risk — patients double-exposed to SJS-risk drugs require extra vigilance. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start carbamazepine 200 mg/day. Continue lamotrigine 200 mg/day. HLA-B*1502 screen BEFORE starting CBZ in Malaysian/Asian patients. Baseline LFTs, FBC, Na⁺. As CBZ is added and uptitrated, LTG levels will fall due to CYP/UGT induction — monitor for mood symptoms indicating subtherapeutic LTG.
Increase carbamazepine to 400 mg/day. Hold lamotrigine. CBZ autoinduction begins. Lamotrigine levels falling — watch for mood breakthrough.
Increase carbamazepine to 600 mg/day. Hold lamotrigine at 200 mg — levels significantly reduced by CBZ induction. CBZ level check if available (autoinduction ongoing).
Increase carbamazepine to 800 mg/day (target). Begin lamotrigine taper: reduce to 150 mg/day. CBZ autoinduction largely complete by week 4 — check CBZ level (target 4–10 mg/L for mood disorder).
Reduce lamotrigine to 100 mg/day. Carbamazepine providing primary cover.
Reduce lamotrigine to 50 mg/day. Almost complete switch.

Stop lamotrigine. Continue carbamazepine 800 mg/day. Recheck CBZ level after lamotrigine is stopped (LTG has minor UGT-inducing effects — minimal change expected but confirm level). Monitor mood stability and bipolar relapse for 3 months.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Not dose-equivalent. Carbamazepine monotherapy target for bipolar: 400–1200 mg/day (serum level 4–10 mg/L). Lamotrigine levels fall during CBZ co-prescription — interpret dose changes in context of the changing PK environment. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

citations: Anderson GD. Pharmacokinetic drug interactions with carbamazepine. Clin Pharmacokinet. 1998.
contraindications: HLA-B*1502 positive (South/South-East Asian patients) — carbamazepine is contraindicated. Prescreening MANDATORY in Malaysian clinical practice.

lamotrigine-to-lithium.rationale: Lamotrigine to lithium: Common switch when stronger mania prevention is needed (lamotrigine has limited anti-manic efficacy — bipolar I patients with recurrent mania may require lithium). No pharmacokinetic interaction between lamotrigine and lithium. Lithium must be titrated to therapeutic level (0.6–1.0 mmol/L) before lamotrigine is reduced. Lamotrigine taper should be gradual (minimum 2 weeks per dose step) to avoid seizure risk (off-label: in patients without epilepsy, abrupt withdrawal still carries theoretical risk and may cause headache, irritability, and insomnia). Mood overlap must be maintained throughout. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start lithium 400 mg/day. Continue lamotrigine 200 mg/day. Baseline renal function, TFT, U&E, ECG (if >40 years). Check lithium level at day 5. Counsel patient about lithium sick-day rules, hydration, avoidance of NSAIDs.
Increase lithium to 800 mg/day if level below target and tolerability confirmed. Continue lamotrigine unchanged. Check lithium level at day 12.
Increase lithium to 1000 mg/day if needed to achieve target 0.6–1.0 mmol/L. Hold lamotrigine at 200 mg/day — full cover maintained.
Lithium confirmed therapeutic. Begin lamotrigine taper: reduce to 150 mg/day. No rapid reductions — maintain gradual taper to avoid withdrawal effects.
Reduce lamotrigine to 100 mg/day. Monitor mood stability.
Reduce lamotrigine to 50 mg/day.

Stop lamotrigine. Continue lithium (dose confirmed by level). Confirm lithium level at 4 and 12 weeks. Note: if patient has bipolar II and lamotrigine was providing antidepressant cover, monitor closely for bipolar depressive relapse — lithium has limited efficacy for bipolar depression compared with lamotrigine.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Not dose-equivalent. Lithium target defined by serum level (0.6–1.0 mmol/L maintenance). Typical maintenance dose 800–1200 mg/day depending on renal function and age. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

contraindications: Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min) — lithium contraindicated.

lamotrigine-to-valproate.rationale: Lamotrigine to valproate: CRITICAL pharmacokinetic interaction — valproate is a potent UGT inhibitor that DOUBLES lamotrigine plasma levels. When valproate is added to lamotrigine, the lamotrigine dose MUST BE HALVED immediately (or before VPA is initiated) to prevent lamotrigine toxicity (diplopia, ataxia, dizziness, rash). Failure to halve the lamotrigine dose when starting valproate is a well-documented prescribing error. Protocol: (1) Halve lamotrigine dose BEFORE or AT THE TIME valproate is started. (2) Titrate valproate to therapeutic dose. (3) Reduce lamotrigine further or stop as valproate reaches maintenance dose. Women of reproductive age: mandatory EURAP/teratogenicity counselling before starting valproate. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: CRITICAL: Halve lamotrigine from 200 mg to 100 mg immediately. Start valproate 500 mg/day simultaneously. Failure to halve LTG causes toxicity (VPA doubles LTG levels). Document EURAP/teratogenicity counselling for women of reproductive age. Baseline LFTs, FBC.
Increase valproate to 1000 mg/day. Hold lamotrigine at 100 mg. This 100 mg dose in the presence of VPA inhibition is equivalent to ~200 mg monotherapy in terms of plasma levels.
Increase valproate to 1500 mg/day (target). Assess lamotrigine tolerability — monitor for diplopia, dizziness, rash.
Reduce lamotrigine to 75 mg/day (clinical context dependent — some patients may be maintained on lamotrigine adjunct with valproate; if full switch planned, continue reducing). Mood stability check.
Reduce lamotrigine to 50 mg/day. Valproate providing primary mood cover.
Stop lamotrigine. Continue valproate 1500 mg/day. Check valproate level if available (target 50–100 mg/L). Metabolic monitoring at 4 and 12 weeks (weight, LFTs, FBC). Bipolar relapse monitoring.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Not dose-equivalent. Lamotrigine 100 mg + valproate 1500 mg is pharmacologically similar to lamotrigine 200 mg monotherapy (VPA doubles LTG levels). Target valproate for mood disorder: 1000–2000 mg/day (level 50–100 mg/L). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

citations: Posner K et al. Lamotrigine plasma levels during coadministration with valproate. Epilepsia. 1991.
contraindications: Current pregnancy or planning pregnancy — valproate is highly teratogenic. Do not switch to valproate in women of reproductive age without EURAP risk minimisation programme and confirmed need.
Allergy or previous serious rash to lamotrigine — monitor at each step; rash risk increases when valproate is combined with lamotrigine.

lithium-to-carbamazepine.rationale: Lithium to carbamazepine: Indicated for rapid cycling bipolar, lithium intolerance/nephropathy, or mixed states. This switch carries two major hazards: (1) Carbamazepine autoinduction — CBZ induces its own metabolism (CYP3A4), so doses must be increased over 4–6 weeks to achieve target levels. Initial doses produce higher levels than final steady-state levels. (2) Neurotoxicity risk during overlap — both lithium and carbamazepine can cause CNS side effects (tremor, ataxia, confusion); the combination carries additive neurotoxic risk even at therapeutic levels. Monitor closely during overlap. (3) Lithium rebound mania risk on rapid withdrawal — taper lithium over at least 4 weeks. Check CBZ level at 2 and 6 weeks (autoinduction reduces levels mid-taper). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start carbamazepine 200 mg/day (CBZ levels will initially be higher — autoinduction not yet active). Continue lithium 1000 mg/day. Check baseline LFTs, FBC, Na⁺, U&E. Warn patient about double CNS effects during overlap phase.
Increase carbamazepine to 400 mg/day. Hold lithium. Autoinduction begins within 1–2 weeks — CBZ levels may actually fall as dose increases due to self-induction.
Increase carbamazepine to 600 mg/day. Hold lithium. Check CBZ level — expected 4–10 mg/L therapeutic range. Also check lithium level. Monitor for neurotoxicity (diplopia, ataxia, confusion).
Reduce lithium to 800 mg/day. Carbamazepine at or near target dose. Autoinduction largely complete by 4 weeks — recheck CBZ level if neurological symptoms present.
Reduce lithium to 400 mg/day. CBZ autoinduction stable. Monitor mood and neurological symptoms.
Reduce lithium to 200 mg/day. CBZ well established. Check CBZ level to confirm therapeutic (4–10 mg/L).

Stop lithium. Continue carbamazepine 800 mg/day. Recheck CBZ level 2 weeks after lithium stopped (stopping lithium removes a CBZ interaction; also confirm autoinduction complete). Monitor for renal function improvement if switch was due to lithium nephropathy.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Not dose-equivalent. Carbamazepine target for bipolar: 400–1200 mg/day titrated to serum level 4–10 mg/L (or higher for some patients with seizure history). Autoinduction means dose must be increased incrementally over 4–6 weeks even after a 'target' is reached. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

contraindications: HLA-B*1502 allele positive (South Asian, South-East Asian ancestry) — carbamazepine contraindicated; SJS risk up to 25× higher. Screen before prescribing in Malaysian patients.
Active bone marrow suppression — carbamazepine causes aplastic anaemia (rare but potentially fatal).

lithium-to-lamotrigine.rationale: Lithium to lamotrigine: Commonly indicated for bipolar II disorder (lamotrigine superior for bipolar II depressive episodes; lithium superior for mania prevention — discuss with patient that lamotrigine has limited anti-manic efficacy). Lamotrigine requires a mandatory slow titration (at least 8–10 weeks to therapeutic dose) to minimise Stevens-Johnson Syndrome risk. Lithium MUST be maintained throughout the entire lamotrigine titration and overlapped until lamotrigine reaches at least 100 mg/day (therapeutic range). Only then should lithium be tapered. Abrupt lithium discontinuation causes rebound mania risk — taper slowly. No pharmacokinetic interaction between lithium and lamotrigine. Total duration approximately 12–14 weeks. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start lamotrigine 25 mg/day (weeks 1–2). Continue lithium 1000 mg/day unchanged. Use the standard (non-VPA-inhibited, non-CBZ-induced) titration schedule. Counsel patient about SJS risk — stop immediately if rash develops and seek urgent review.
Increase lamotrigine to 50 mg/day (weeks 3–4). Hold lithium. No dose change in lithium — full cover maintained.
Increase lamotrigine to 100 mg/day (weeks 5–6). Hold lithium. Lamotrigine now at minimum therapeutic dose — continue overlap for consolidation.
Increase lamotrigine to 150 mg/day. Begin lithium taper: reduce lithium to 800 mg/day. Check lithium level. Lamotrigine now providing meaningful mood cover.
Increase lamotrigine to 200 mg/day (target maintenance dose). Reduce lithium to 600 mg/day. Monitor for early mood symptoms during lithium reduction.
Reduce lithium to 400 mg/day. Lamotrigine consolidated at 200 mg/day. Further lithium taper safe if stable.

Stop lithium. Continue lamotrigine 200 mg/day. Note: lamotrigine has limited mania prevention efficacy — counsel patient to have a relapse prevention plan. Monitor for manic symptoms for 3 months post-lithium withdrawal.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Not dose-equivalent. Lamotrigine maintenance target for bipolar disorder: 100–200 mg/day (monotherapy). Slow titration is mandatory (SJS risk) — cannot compress schedule below Maudsley/SPC minimum rates. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

lithium-to-valproate.rationale: Lithium to valproate: Common switch for intolerance, renal impairment, or bipolar II with mixed features (where valproate may be preferred). Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and abrupt withdrawal precipitates rebound mania — taper over at least 4–6 weeks. Overlap with valproate is essential to prevent mood relapse. No pharmacokinetic interaction between lithium and valproate. Valproate takes 1–2 weeks to reach steady state at each dose level. Monitor lithium levels during taper and discontinue below therapeutic range only once valproate is established at therapeutic dose. Women of reproductive age: mandatory EURAP/teratogenicity counselling before initiating valproate. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start valproate 500 mg/day (or sodium valproate 200 mg BD). Continue lithium 1000 mg/day. Baseline LFTs, FBC. EURAP/teratogenicity counselling documented for women of reproductive age. No PK interaction — safe to overlap.
Increase valproate to 1000 mg/day. Continue lithium unchanged. Check valproate tolerability (GI side effects, sedation).
Increase valproate to 1500 mg/day (target for most patients). Begin lithium taper: reduce to 800 mg/day. Check lithium level.
Reduce lithium to 600 mg/day. Valproate at therapeutic dose. Monitor for mood symptoms indicating subtherapeutic lithium cover.
Reduce lithium to 400 mg/day. Check lithium level — expected to be sub-therapeutic by now. Patient must be monitored for early relapse signs.
Reduce lithium to 200 mg/day. Final step before discontinuation. Valproate level if clinically indicated.

Stop lithium. Continue valproate 1500 mg/day. Confirm valproate level if available (target 50–100 mg/L for mood). Monitor renal function improvement if switch driven by lithium nephropathy. Relapse risk remains elevated for 3 months post-lithium.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Not directly dose-equivalent. Lithium 1000 mg/day → valproate 1000–2000 mg/day titrated to therapeutic serum level (50–100 mg/L) and clinical response. Dose above uses 1500 mg as a typical mid-range target. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

contraindications: Current pregnancy — valproate is teratogenic; discuss safer alternatives (e.g. quetiapine, lithium dose reduction) with specialist.
Planning pregnancy — teratogenicity counselling and EURAP risk minimisation programme required before starting valproate in women of reproductive age.

lurasidone-to-aripiprazole.rationale: Lurasidone (D2 full antagonist) to aripiprazole (D2/D3 partial agonist). Both drugs have low metabolic risk and low QTc risk — a good lateral switch for patients prioritising a clean metabolic and cardiac profile. Common reasons: food adherence difficulties with lurasidone, cost, or desire for aripiprazole's mood-stabilising augmentation profile. Aripiprazole's partial D2 agonism may cause akathisia, particularly in the first 2–4 weeks, in patients stabilised on full D2 blockade. Cross-taper preferred over direct switch to allow gradual receptor adaptation. Activation and insomnia are also common on aripiprazole initiation. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start aripiprazole 10 mg. Continue lurasidone 80 mg with main meal. Counsel about akathisia risk in first 2 weeks — restlessness, inability to sit still. Propranolol PRN can be prescribed proactively.
Increase aripiprazole to 15 mg (target). Reduce lurasidone to 40 mg. Review akathisia at end of week 1.
Reduce lurasidone to 20 mg. Aripiprazole at steady state. Insomnia may emerge as lurasidone's mild sedation is lost.
Stop lurasidone. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Prolactin normalises rapidly — counsel female patients about menstrual restoration.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Lurasidone 80 mg ≈ aripiprazole 15 mg (inferred from DDD equivalence; limited direct data). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

lurasidone-to-haloperidol.rationale: Lurasidone (SGA, low EPS, low QTc) to haloperidol (FGA, high EPS, moderate QTc). An uncommon switch typically driven by need for IM administration (acute psychosis), cost, or formulary constraints. The EPS burden increases significantly with haloperidol — particularly dystonia risk in young males and akathisia. Anticholinergic prophylaxis (procyclidine) should be prescribed PRN. QTc rises on haloperidol — ECG required. Both drugs have moderate prolactin elevation; prolactin may increase further on haloperidol. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start haloperidol 2 mg. Continue lurasidone 80 mg with main meal. Baseline ECG. Prescribe procyclidine 5 mg PRN for acute dystonia — particularly important for young males. Warn about EPS risk.
Increase haloperidol to 4 mg. Reduce lurasidone to 40 mg. Monitor for EPS — stiffness, akathisia. If EPS develops, consider lower haloperidol dose rather than adding long-term anticholinergics.
Reduce lurasidone to 20 mg. Haloperidol at target. Check ECG at 2 weeks.
Stop lurasidone. Continue haloperidol 4 mg. Repeat ECG at 4–6 weeks. Monitor for tardive dyskinesia risk with long-term haloperidol use.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Lurasidone 80 mg ≈ haloperidol 4 mg (inferred from DDD equivalence: both ≈ olanzapine 10 mg by proxy). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

lurasidone-to-olanzapine.rationale: Lurasidone (low metabolic risk, low QTc risk, food requirement) to olanzapine (high metabolic risk, high sedation, no food requirement). Common reasons: insufficient response to lurasidone, need for more sedation, or patient non-compliance with food requirement. The switch moves the patient toward higher metabolic risk — baseline metabolic parameters must be documented. Lurasidone has no significant anticholinergic activity so withdrawal is gentle; the main clinical change will be the increase in sedation from olanzapine's H1 and M1 blockade. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start olanzapine 5 mg nocte. Continue lurasidone 80 mg with main meal. Record baseline weight, fasting glucose, fasting lipids before starting olanzapine.
Increase olanzapine to 10 mg nocte (target). Plateau lurasidone. Sedation increases significantly — advise patient on driving and daytime drowsiness.
Reduce lurasidone to 40 mg. Olanzapine at steady state and target dose. No cholinergic rebound from lurasidone reduction.
Reduce lurasidone to 20 mg. Transition nearing completion.
Stop lurasidone. Continue olanzapine 10 mg nocte. Schedule metabolic review at 4 and 12 weeks. Weight gain expected — dietary and exercise counselling.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Lurasidone 80 mg ≈ olanzapine 10 mg (inferred from DDD equivalence: both ≈ olanzapine 10 mg by proxy; limited direct published data for lurasidone equivalence). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

lurasidone-to-quetiapine.rationale: Lurasidone (weight-neutral, low sedation, food-dependent) to quetiapine (moderate-high sedation, moderate metabolic risk, antidepressant augmentation effect via norquetiapine). Common reasons: patient cannot reliably eat with medication (food requirement problematic), desire for more sedation or better sleep, or switching to quetiapine for its antidepressant augmentation in bipolar depression. Quetiapine initiation should be nocte — sedation onset is immediate. Postural hypotension is common on quetiapine initiation. Metabolic risk increases on quetiapine — baseline measures before starting. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start quetiapine 100 mg nocte. Continue lurasidone 80 mg with main meal. Record baseline weight, fasting glucose, fasting lipids. Warn about postural hypotension on quetiapine initiation.
Increase quetiapine to 200 mg nocte. Plateau lurasidone. Sedation increases — warn about daytime drowsiness. Orthostasis diminishing as tolerance develops.
Increase quetiapine to 400 mg (target — or titrate further if needed). Reduce lurasidone to 40 mg.
Reduce lurasidone to 20 mg. Quetiapine well established. No cholinergic rebound from lurasidone reduction.
Stop lurasidone. Continue quetiapine 400 mg. Metabolic monitoring at 4 and 12 weeks. Weight gain expected.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Lurasidone 80 mg ≈ quetiapine 400 mg (inferred from DDD equivalence; limited direct data). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

lurasidone-to-risperidone.rationale: Lurasidone (D2, 5-HT2A, 5-HT7, partial 5-HT1A) to risperidone (D2/D3 + 5-HT2A + α1/α2 + H1). Common reasons: formulary, cost, or need for LAI (risperidone LAI or paliperidone LAI available). Relatively straightforward switch — both are moderate-sedation SGAs. Prolactin will rise on risperidone (lurasidone raises prolactin moderately). Both drugs have minimal anticholinergic activity so cross-taper can proceed at a standard pace. QTc: risperidone has moderate QTc effect (less than amisulpride/haloperidol) and lurasidone has minimal — net QTc neutral to slight increase; ECG if risk factors. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start risperidone 2 mg. Continue lurasidone 80 mg with main meal. Baseline clinical assessment.
Increase risperidone to 4 mg (target). Reduce lurasidone to 40 mg. Prolactin elevation likely increasing as risperidone titrates up.
Reduce lurasidone to 20 mg. Risperidone at target dose. Clinical stability should be maintained.
Stop lurasidone. Continue risperidone 4 mg. Prolactin elevation expected — check if LAI transition is planned for next step.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Lurasidone 80 mg ≈ risperidone 4 mg (inferred from DDD equivalence; limited direct lurasidone equivalence data). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

mirtazapine-to-agomelatine.rationale: Mirtazapine (NaSSA: α2-antagonist, 5-HT2/3 antagonist, H1 blocker; t½ ~20–40h; sedating; significant weight gain) to agomelatine (MT1/MT2 agonist; t½ ~2h; weight neutral; much less sedating). Switch reasons: weight gain, excessive sedation, or metabolic concerns on mirtazapine. As mirtazapine is reduced, H1 blockade and noradrenergic effects reduce — insomnia may re-emerge (agomelatine helps sleep but less potently than mirtazapine's H1 blockade). No pharmacodynamic serotonin syndrome risk. Baseline LFTs before starting agomelatine. Taper mirtazapine to avoid sleep disruption during withdrawal. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start agomelatine 25 mg nocte (same time as mirtazapine). Continue mirtazapine 30 mg. CHECK BASELINE LFTs. Warn: sleep quality may temporarily worsen as mirtazapine is reduced (H1 blockade being withdrawn). Agomelatine will help sleep continuity but is less sedating.
Reduce mirtazapine to 15 mg. Continue agomelatine 25 mg. Monitor sleep and mood. Some rebound insomnia possible.

Stop mirtazapine. Continue agomelatine 25 mg nocte. Sleep may be lighter than on mirtazapine — set expectations. Titrate agomelatine to 50 mg at 2 weeks if response inadequate. Appetite and weight should begin to normalise over 4–8 weeks.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Mirtazapine 30 mg → agomelatine 25 mg (start dose). Not pharmacologically equivalent — different mechanisms. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

contraindications: Hepatic impairment — agomelatine contraindicated.
ALT >3× ULN at baseline — do not start agomelatine.

mirtazapine-to-desvenlafaxine.rationale: Mirtazapine (NaSSA; t½ ~20–40h; heavy sedation; significant weight gain) to desvenlafaxine (SNRI; t½ ~11h; weight neutral; activating). Switch reasons: weight gain, excessive sedation, or inadequate antidepressant response. Switching FROM mirtazapine TO an activating SNRI: expect reduced sedation and appetite as mirtazapine is tapered — insomnia may emerge temporarily. Desvenlafaxine's noradrenergic activity during cross-taper combined with mirtazapine's α2-antagonism: additive noradrenergic stimulation possible — monitor for agitation, tachycardia. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start desvenlafaxine 50 mg. Continue mirtazapine 30 mg nocte. Monitor for additive noradrenergic effects during overlap (agitation, sweating, tachycardia). Counsel patient: sleep quality may worsen and appetite will reduce as mirtazapine is tapered.
Reduce mirtazapine to 15 mg nocte. Continue desvenlafaxine 50 mg. Rebound insomnia possible — short-term sleep hygiene advice. Monitor mood.

Stop mirtazapine. Continue desvenlafaxine 50 mg. Sleep will likely improve over 2–4 weeks as pharmacology normalises. Weight reduction expected over months. Titrate desvenlafaxine to 100 mg at 4 weeks if response inadequate.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Mirtazapine 30 mg → desvenlafaxine 50 mg (standard effective doses). Not pharmacologically equivalent — different mechanisms. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

mirtazapine-to-escitalopram.rationale: Deprescribing mirtazapine while moving to a single SSRI. Different mechanisms (NaSSA vs SSRI) so direct serotonin-syndrome risk is low; main concern is rebound insomnia/anxiety as mirtazapine is reduced. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start escitalopram 5 mg in the morning. Hold mirtazapine 30 mg at night.
Hold mirtazapine. Increase escitalopram to 10 mg target.
Halve mirtazapine to 15 mg. Counsel re possible rebound insomnia.
Stop mirtazapine. Continue escitalopram 10 mg. If significant insomnia emerges, consider short overlap or alternative sleep strategy.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Mirtazapine and escitalopram are not directly equipotent — the mapping reflects typical effective doses for major depression. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

mirtazapine-to-sertraline.rationale: Common scenario: mirtazapine was used for short-term sleep/appetite effect or as augmentation, and the patient is moving to a single SSRI. Mechanisms are different (NaSSA vs SSRI) so direct serotonin-syndrome risk is low, but rebound insomnia and anxiety can occur on mirtazapine cessation. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start sertraline 25 mg in the morning. Hold mirtazapine 30 mg at night.
Hold mirtazapine. Increase sertraline to 50 mg.
Halve mirtazapine to 15 mg. Increase sertraline to 100 mg target. Counsel patient about possible rebound insomnia.
Stop mirtazapine. Continue sertraline 100 mg. If significant insomnia emerges, consider a short overlap of mirtazapine 7.5 mg or alternative sleep strategy.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Mirtazapine and sertraline are not directly equipotent — the mapping reflects typical effective doses for major depression. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

mirtazapine-to-vortioxetine.rationale: Mirtazapine (NaSSA; t½ ~20–40h; H1 blockade causing heavy sedation and weight gain) to vortioxetine (SMS; t½ ~66h; cognitive benefits; weight neutral; minimal sedation). Switch reasons: excessive weight gain, sedation, or cognitive blunting on mirtazapine. As mirtazapine is tapered, sedation and appetite stimulation will reduce — insomnia and weight normalisation expected. Vortioxetine provides serotonergic cover during the transition. No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start vortioxetine 10 mg. Continue mirtazapine 30 mg. Patients may notice cognitive improvement from vortioxetine during the overlap phase. Counsel: sleep may worsen as mirtazapine is reduced (H1 sedation being withdrawn).
Reduce mirtazapine to 15 mg. Hold vortioxetine. Some rebound insomnia possible — advise short-term sleep hygiene measures.
Stop mirtazapine. Continue vortioxetine 10 mg. Sleep likely improved over 2–4 weeks as pharmacology normalises. Weight will reduce over months. Titrate vortioxetine to 20 mg if response inadequate.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Mirtazapine 30 mg → vortioxetine 10 mg (start dose; titrate to 20 mg). Not pharmacologically equivalent — different mechanisms. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

olanzapine-to-amisulpride.rationale: Olanzapine (high anticholinergic, antihistaminergic, and antiadrenergic burden) to amisulpride (selective D2/D3, no anticholinergic activity). Common reasons: metabolic syndrome on olanzapine, weight gain, sexual dysfunction (amisulpride raises prolactin but does not cause weight gain), or QTc needs — note amisulpride also prolongs QTc. Olanzapine withdrawal must be gradual to avoid cholinergic rebound (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, diaphoresis, insomnia). The patient will notice the loss of sedation — insomnia is common in the first 2–4 weeks and should be anticipated. Metabolic improvement (weight loss, lipid/glucose normalisation) typically occurs over weeks to months after olanzapine cessation. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start amisulpride 200 mg. Continue olanzapine 10 mg. Obtain baseline ECG (amisulpride can prolong QTc). Check renal function (amisulpride is renally excreted).
Increase amisulpride to 400 mg (target). Plateau olanzapine. Allow amisulpride to approach steady state before tapering the highly anticholinergic olanzapine.
Reduce olanzapine to 7.5 mg. Watch for cholinergic rebound — nausea, sweating, insomnia. If rebound is severe, slow the olanzapine taper. Sedation begins to reduce.
Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg. Insomnia or increased anxiety may emerge as histamine blockade is lost. Short-term use of promethazine or melatonin can bridge sleep difficulties.
Stop olanzapine. Continue amisulpride 400 mg. Repeat ECG at 4–6 weeks. Monitor weight and metabolic parameters at 4 and 12 weeks (improvement expected but not immediate).

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Olanzapine 10 mg ≈ amisulpride 400 mg (Leucht et al. CMD method, Schizophrenia Bulletin 2015). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

olanzapine-to-aripiprazole-lai.rationale: A common clinically motivated switch combining two goals: escaping olanzapine's very high metabolic burden (weight gain, glycaemic risk) AND gaining the adherence benefits of a monthly LAI. Aripiprazole LAI (Abilify Maintena) requires a mandatory 14-day oral aripiprazole overlap after the first injection. Plateau cross-taper: start the first Maintena injection (+ oral aripiprazole overlap), then taper olanzapine only after the oral overlap is complete and the depot is therapeutic. This prevents both a coverage gap and a period where high akathisia risk from aripiprazole coincides with inadequate olanzapine cover. Akathisia risk is substantial: aripiprazole's D2 partial agonism acting on a receptor pool previously saturated by olanzapine. Counsel early and watch closely. Metabolic improvement should be tracked prospectively — weight and glucose at 4 and 12 weeks. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Administer Abilify Maintena 400 mg IM. Start oral aripiprazole 10 mg/day — 14-day oral overlap MANDATORY. Continue olanzapine 10 mg. Warn patient about akathisia — advise to report restlessness.
Day 7: Continue oral aripiprazole 10 mg + olanzapine 10 mg. Assess akathisia. Depot reaching therapeutic levels. Sedation additive — advise on driving.
STOP oral aripiprazole (14-day overlap complete). Depot now therapeutic. Begin tapering olanzapine to 7.5 mg. Cholinergic/histaminergic rebound possible as olanzapine reduces.
Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg. Metabolic improvement beginning. Monitor sleep — olanzapine's H1 antihistaminergic sedation diminishing.
Stop olanzapine. Second Maintena 400 mg injection. Confirm akathisia absent or managed. Document baseline metabolics — weight, fasting glucose, lipids.
Ongoing: monthly Maintena 400 mg. Weight and glucose at 4 and 12 weeks. Metabolic improvement expected 3–6 months after olanzapine cessation.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: olanzapine 10 mg ≈ aripiprazole LAI 400 mg/4 weeks (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table + LAI conversion). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

olanzapine-to-aripiprazole.rationale: Common metabolically-driven switch (escape weight gain, dyslipidaemia, glycaemic concern). Plateau cross-taper is preferred over straight cross-taper because olanzapine's strong anticholinergic and antihistaminergic activity creates cholinergic and histaminergic rebound on rapid reduction; aripiprazole's partial agonism can provoke akathisia, especially when superimposed on a fully antagonised D2 receptor pool. Slow taper of olanzapine after aripiprazole stabilisation gives the cleanest transition. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start aripiprazole 5 mg in the morning. Hold olanzapine 10 mg at night.
Increase aripiprazole to 10 mg. Hold olanzapine. Watch for akathisia.
Increase aripiprazole to 15 mg target. Begin reducing olanzapine to 7.5 mg.
Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg. Hold aripiprazole 15 mg.
Reduce olanzapine to 2.5 mg. Counsel about cholinergic rebound symptoms.
Stop olanzapine. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg. Slow this final step if rebound emerges.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: olanzapine 10 mg ≈ aripiprazole 15 mg (Maudsley 14th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

olanzapine-to-haloperidol.rationale: SGA-to-FGA switch — uncommon in modern practice but clinically encountered for cost-driven reasons, or when adequate psychotic control requires high D2 occupancy beyond the SGA ceiling. Moving from olanzapine to haloperidol trades metabolic burden for EPS risk: anticipate EPS emergence (parkinsonism, akathisia) as haloperidol establishes. Anticipate anticholinergic and histaminergic withdrawal as olanzapine tapers — rebound insomnia and cholinergic effects are likely. Consider prophylactic anticholinergic cover (benzhexol) before starting haloperidol in patients with EPS history. QTc will rise — ECG at baseline is mandatory for haloperidol. Start haloperidol at a conservative 2 mg and assess for EPS before stepping to target. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start haloperidol 2 mg. Continue olanzapine 10 mg. Baseline ECG mandatory — haloperidol is a high QTc risk drug. Assess EPS at every step.
Increase haloperidol to 5 mg (target). Plateau olanzapine — allow haloperidol to establish before tapering the anticholinergic SGA cover.
Begin tapering olanzapine to 7.5 mg. Monitor for cholinergic/histaminergic rebound — insomnia, GI symptoms, anxiety. Consider anticholinergic cover if EPS already emerging.
Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg. Haloperidol's antipsychotic effect now dominant. Review EPS — prescribe benzhexol if needed.
Stop olanzapine. Continue haloperidol 5 mg. Metabolic parameters should improve — document weight and glucose as baseline for comparison. Recheck QTc.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: olanzapine 10 mg ≈ haloperidol 5 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

olanzapine-to-lurasidone.rationale: Olanzapine (high metabolic risk, strong anticholinergic, antihistaminergic) to lurasidone (weight-neutral, low QTc, food-dependent). Common reason: metabolic syndrome on olanzapine — weight gain, dyslipidaemia, glucose dysregulation. Lurasidone is one of the most metabolically neutral antipsychotics. Critical: lurasidone must be taken with at least 350 kcal food — this must be explicitly taught before starting. Olanzapine withdrawal must be gradual to manage cholinergic rebound and to avoid abrupt loss of H1-mediated sedation (insomnia). Weight loss and metabolic improvement occur gradually over weeks to months. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start lurasidone 40 mg with the main meal. Continue olanzapine 10 mg. CRITICAL counselling: lurasidone must be taken with ≥350 kcal of food every day — bioavailability is halved without food.
Increase lurasidone to 80 mg with main meal. Plateau olanzapine. Food counselling reinforcement — check patient understands the requirement.
Reduce olanzapine to 7.5 mg. Cholinergic rebound risk — nausea, insomnia, sweating. Go slowly if rebound is symptomatic. Loss of sedation begins.
Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg. Insomnia may be prominent. Short-term melatonin or promethazine can bridge sleep. Lurasidone well established by now.
Stop olanzapine. Continue lurasidone 80 mg with main meal. Monitor weight and metabolic parameters at 4, 12, and 26 weeks — improvement expected but gradual.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Olanzapine 10 mg ≈ lurasidone 80 mg (inferred from DDD equivalence; limited direct lurasidone equivalence data). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

olanzapine-to-paliperidone-lai.rationale: Common transition for patients on oral olanzapine who need improved adherence via depot, but where the metabolic burden of olanzapine is being tolerated or is less of a concern than non-adherence. Paliperidone palmitate (Invega Sustenna) uses a deltoid loading protocol (150 mg day 1, 100 mg day 8) that eliminates the need for a separate oral overlap period — the loading doses reach therapeutic concentrations quickly. Oral olanzapine is therefore tapered DURING the PP-LAI loading period, not stopped beforehand. Cholinergic and histaminergic rebound from olanzapine reduction is monitored; paliperidone's lower anticholinergic activity means partial rebound symptoms (insomnia, anxiety) are possible. CYP interactions: olanzapine's CYP1A2 substrate status means smokers on olanzapine may need upward dose review of paliperidone if co-medications change. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: PP-LAI loading dose 1: 150 mg deltoid (MUST be deltoid for loading). Continue oral olanzapine 10 mg. Advise patient that PP-LAI needs 2 loading injections to establish therapeutic levels.
PP-LAI loading dose 2: 100 mg deltoid (day 8 ± 2 days). Continue oral olanzapine 10 mg. PP-LAI levels are building.
PP-LAI reaching therapeutic concentration. Begin tapering oral olanzapine to 5 mg. Monitor for cholinergic/histaminergic rebound symptoms (insomnia, anxiety) as olanzapine reduces.

Stop oral olanzapine. PP-LAI first maintenance injection (100 mg deltoid or gluteal, due day 36-38 after first loading dose). Monthly maintenance thereafter. Review metabolic parameters — paliperidone has lower metabolic burden than olanzapine.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: oral olanzapine 10 mg ≈ paliperidone palmitate 100 mg monthly (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

olanzapine-to-quetiapine.rationale: Olanzapine-to-quetiapine switches are usually laterally metabolic — accepting the same class of metabolic burden while gaining quetiapine-specific benefits (antidepressant effect from N-desalkylquetiapine, improved tolerability in patients distressed by weight gain at olanzapine levels, or reduced prolactin effect). Both drugs are strongly sedating and anticholinergic/antihistaminergic, so rebound on withdrawal is less pronounced than with less sedating APs. Cross-taper: introduce quetiapine nocte alongside olanzapine before tapering, to prevent a sedation and antipsychotic coverage gap. Metabolic monitoring continues — no meaningful metabolic improvement is expected, though individual response varies. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start quetiapine 50 mg nocte. Continue olanzapine 10 mg. Sedation is additive initially — advise driving caution.
Increase quetiapine to 100 mg. Plateau olanzapine — allow quetiapine to establish before tapering.
Increase quetiapine to 200 mg. Begin tapering olanzapine to 7.5 mg. If daytime sedation excessive, consider splitting quetiapine dose.
Quetiapine at 300 mg target. Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg. Antipsychotic cover well-maintained across both agents at this step.
Stop olanzapine. Continue quetiapine 300 mg. Continue metabolic monitoring — QTc is moderate risk with quetiapine.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: olanzapine 10 mg ≈ quetiapine 300 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

olanzapine-to-risperidone.rationale: Considered when metabolic burden of olanzapine outweighs prolactin/EPS concerns of risperidone. Plateau cross-taper to manage cholinergic/histaminergic rebound on the olanzapine side. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start risperidone 1 mg at night. Hold olanzapine 10 mg.
Increase risperidone to 2 mg. Hold olanzapine.
Reduce olanzapine to 7.5 mg. Increase risperidone to 3 mg.
Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg. Increase risperidone to 4 mg target.
Stop olanzapine. Continue risperidone 4 mg. Counsel about possible cholinergic rebound and rising prolactin.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: olanzapine 10 mg ≈ risperidone 4 mg (Maudsley 14th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

paliperidone-lai-to-aripiprazole-lai.rationale: SGA-to-SGA depot switch, most commonly driven by metabolic concerns (weight gain, glycaemic deterioration) or hyperprolactinaemia (sexual dysfunction, galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, bone density concern). Aripiprazole LAI (Abilify Maintena) requires a mandatory 14-day oral aripiprazole overlap after the first injection. Paliperidone palmitate's long half-life (~25-49 days) provides seamless D2 cover during the oral overlap period and beyond — no coverage gap. Akathisia risk: as aripiprazole's D2 partial agonism replaces paliperidone's full antagonism, akathisia is the main switch concern. Counsel the patient early. Prolactin will drop substantially — patients with hyperprolactinaemia-related symptoms should notice improvement within weeks. Metabolic parameters (weight, glucose, lipids) should improve progressively as aripiprazole's metabolically neutral profile takes over. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Administer Abilify Maintena 400 mg IM (gluteal or deltoid) in place of next scheduled Sustenna. Do NOT give Sustenna today. Start oral aripiprazole 10 mg daily — 14-day oral overlap MANDATORY. PP-LAI tail continues releasing. Counsel patient about akathisia risk.
STOP oral aripiprazole today (14-day overlap complete). Abilify Maintena now therapeutic. PP-LAI clearing. Prolactin should already be falling. Monitor for akathisia.
Second Maintena 400 mg injection. PP-LAI substantially cleared. Review prolactin, metabolic parameters, akathisia. Monthly Maintena thereafter.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: paliperidone palmitate 100 mg/4 weeks ≈ aripiprazole LAI 400 mg/4 weeks (Maudsley 15th, LAI equivalence). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

paliperidone-lai-to-paliperidone.rationale: Switching from Invega Sustenna (PP1M) to oral paliperidone (Invega). The depot continues releasing paliperidone for up to 4–5 months after the last injection; oral paliperidone supplements then eventually replaces this release. Start oral at a dose equivalent to the monthly depot dose and allow the depot tail to naturally taper. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Skip the next scheduled PP1M injection. Start oral paliperidone at approximately equivalent dose (75 mg eq/month ≈ 6 mg/day oral). Depot continues releasing — monitor for dual-drug effects initially.
Depot level falling. Continue oral paliperidone 6 mg/day. No second injection given.
Depot level substantially reduced. Oral paliperidone now primary contributor. Assess clinical response — consider dose adjustment if needed.
Depot largely cleared (~3 months post-last-injection). Oral paliperidone as near-monotherapy.
Depot cleared (~4–5 months post-last-injection). Oral paliperidone monotherapy established. Review and adjust oral dose based on clinical response.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Invega Sustenna 75 mg eq/month ≈ oral paliperidone 6 mg/day (Maudsley 15th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

safetyFlags.title: Extended depot tail
safetyFlags.body: Paliperidone palmitate has an effective t½ of ~25–49 days. Plasma levels persist for up to 4–5 months after the final injection. Dose the oral supplement conservatively to avoid combined toxicity early in the switch.

safetyFlags.title: Renal function
safetyFlags.body: Paliperidone is primarily renally cleared. Monitor renal function — adjust oral dose if CrCl declines.

paroxetine-to-escitalopram.rationale: Common escape from paroxetine to a gentler SSRI with cleaner pharmacokinetics. Slow paroxetine taper required given high discontinuation-syndrome and anticholinergic-rebound risk. Escitalopram is started at 5 mg and titrated as paroxetine is reduced. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start escitalopram 5 mg in the morning. Hold paroxetine 20 mg.
Halve paroxetine to 10 mg. Increase escitalopram to 10 mg target. Counsel patient about possible discontinuation symptoms.
Hold both. Allow stabilisation.
Stop paroxetine. Continue escitalopram 10 mg. If discontinuation symptoms emerge, slow this final step or use compounded liquid paroxetine.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: paroxetine 20 mg ≈ escitalopram 10 mg (Maudsley 14th). Hyperbolic-tapering principles favour smaller-than-linear final steps. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

paroxetine-to-fluoxetine.rationale: ‘Fluoxetine bridge’ technique: starting fluoxetine while reducing paroxetine, leveraging fluoxetine's long half-life and norfluoxetine metabolite to smooth paroxetine discontinuation symptoms. Particularly useful for patients with prior failed paroxetine tapers or marked discontinuation sensitivity. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start fluoxetine 20 mg in the morning. Hold paroxetine 20 mg.
Halve paroxetine to 10 mg. Hold fluoxetine 20 mg. Fluoxetine has not yet reached steady state but is starting to substitute receptor occupancy.
Hold both. Allow stabilisation.
Stop paroxetine. Fluoxetine + norfluoxetine cover any residual paroxetine-withdrawal effect over the following weeks. Counsel patient about a future 5-week MAOI washout if relevant.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: paroxetine 20 mg ≈ fluoxetine 20 mg (Maudsley 14th). The fluoxetine bridge commits the patient to a 5-week washout before any future MAOI — flag this in the discharge plan. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

paroxetine-to-sertraline.rationale: Common scenario: switching off paroxetine to escape its high discontinuation-syndrome and anticholinergic burden, while preserving SSRI cover. Slow taper essential because paroxetine has short half-life and severe withdrawal risk. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start sertraline 25 mg in the morning. Hold paroxetine 20 mg.
Halve paroxetine to 10 mg. Increase sertraline to 50 mg. Warn patient about possible discontinuation symptoms.
Hold paroxetine 10 mg. Increase sertraline to 100 mg target.
Stop paroxetine. Continue sertraline 100 mg. If discontinuation symptoms emerge, slow this final step or use compounded liquid paroxetine for a longer taper.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: paroxetine 20 mg ≈ sertraline 100 mg (Maudsley 14th). Hyperbolic tapering principles favour smaller-than-linear final steps; consider compounded liquid for patients with prior failed paroxetine tapers. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

quetiapine-to-amisulpride.rationale: Quetiapine (high anticholinergic, antihistaminergic, and antiadrenergic burden) to amisulpride (selective D2/D3). Quetiapine's receptor-binding profile is dominated by H1, muscarinic, and α1 blockade — withdrawal produces significant cholinergic rebound (nausea, insomnia, diarrhoea). The taper must be slow. Loss of quetiapine's sedative effect will cause insomnia in most patients — anticipate and manage proactively. Both drugs prolong QTc; the total QTc burden peaks during overlap. Prolactin will rise on amisulpride (quetiapine is relatively prolactin-sparing). Metabolic improvement expected as quetiapine is withdrawn. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start amisulpride 200 mg. Continue quetiapine 400 mg. Baseline ECG. Check renal function (amisulpride renally excreted). Warn about likely insomnia as quetiapine is reduced.
Increase amisulpride to 400 mg (target). Plateau quetiapine. Monitor QTc at peak overlap — check ECG if combined risk factors present.
Reduce quetiapine to 200 mg. Cholinergic rebound likely now: nausea, sweating, disturbed sleep. Do not rush this taper. Melatonin or antihistamine (e.g. promethazine) may help with sleep.
Reduce quetiapine to 100 mg. Sedation reducing substantially. Postural hypotension from α1 blockade reducing — orthostasis risk diminishes.
Stop quetiapine. Continue amisulpride 400 mg. Repeat ECG at 4–6 weeks. Monitor weight and metabolic parameters — improvement expected over subsequent months.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Quetiapine 400 mg ≈ amisulpride 400 mg (Leucht et al. CMD method, Schizophrenia Bulletin 2015). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

quetiapine-to-aripiprazole-lai.rationale: A clinically common switch combining adherence improvement (LAI) with metabolic improvement (escaping quetiapine's high metabolic burden and sedation). Aripiprazole LAI (Abilify Maintena) requires a mandatory 14-day oral aripiprazole overlap after the first injection. Plateau cross-taper: administer Maintena with the oral overlap while keeping quetiapine at its current dose, then taper quetiapine only after the oral overlap completes and the depot is at therapeutic levels. Quetiapine's discontinuation syndrome is clinically significant — rebound insomnia and anxiety via histaminergic (H1) and α1-adrenergic withdrawal become pronounced as doses fall below 200 mg. Taper slowly through the final 200–100 mg steps. Akathisia risk from aripiprazole is substantial when D2 receptors have been heavily occupied by quetiapine — warn the patient early and have a low threshold to add a short-course propranolol. Metabolic improvement (weight, glucose, lipids) typically begins 4–8 weeks after quetiapine is stopped. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Administer Abilify Maintena 400 mg IM (deltoid or gluteal). Start oral aripiprazole 10 mg/day — 14-day oral overlap MANDATORY. Continue quetiapine 400 mg. Warn patient about akathisia — advise to report restlessness immediately. Do NOT reduce quetiapine yet.
Day 7 check: Continue oral aripiprazole 10 mg + quetiapine 400 mg. Depot reaching therapeutic levels. Assess akathisia. Sedation remains from quetiapine — advise on driving.

STOP oral aripiprazole (14-day overlap complete). Depot now therapeutic. Begin tapering quetiapine to 200 mg. Warn patient: this is the step most likely to trigger H1/α1 rebound — insomnia and anxiety are common. Sleep hygiene advice.
Reduce quetiapine to 100 mg. Rebound insomnia risk is high at this step. Consider temporary low-dose melatonin if sleep significantly disrupted. Metabolic improvement beginning — document weight.
Stop quetiapine completely. Second Maintena injection due today (400 mg). Confirm akathisia absent or managed. Baseline metabolics: weight, fasting glucose, lipids.
Ongoing: monthly Maintena 400 mg. Weight and glucose at 4 and 12 weeks post-quetiapine-cessation. Full metabolic improvement expected over 3–6 months.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: quetiapine 400 mg/day ≈ aripiprazole LAI 400 mg/4 weeks (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table + LAI conversion). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

quetiapine-to-aripiprazole.rationale: Common when sedation, weight gain, or insufficient antipsychotic effect at high quetiapine doses drives a switch. Plateau cross-taper because quetiapine's strong antihistaminergic and α1-adrenergic activity creates rebound insomnia, anxiety and orthostasis on rapid reduction. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start aripiprazole 5 mg in the morning. Hold quetiapine 400 mg at night.
Increase aripiprazole to 10 mg. Hold quetiapine. Counsel re likely improvement in daytime sedation.
Increase aripiprazole to 15 mg. Reduce quetiapine to 300 mg.
Reduce quetiapine to 200 mg. Watch for rebound insomnia at the lower-end histaminergic doses.
Reduce quetiapine to 100 mg. Sleep hygiene advice; consider short-term hypnotic if rebound insomnia.
Stop quetiapine. Continue aripiprazole 15 mg.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: quetiapine 400 mg ≈ aripiprazole 15 mg (Maudsley 14th). Equivalency for low-dose (≤200 mg) quetiapine used purely for sleep is poorly defined. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

quetiapine-to-haloperidol.rationale: SGA-to-FGA switch with significant rebound risk from quetiapine. Plateau cross-taper: introduce haloperidol first and stabilise before tapering quetiapine, because quetiapine's potent H1 and α1-adrenergic antagonism produces marked rebound insomnia, anxiety and orthostatic hypotension on rapid reduction. Allow haloperidol to reach target (5 mg) before quetiapine taper begins. Baseline ECG is mandatory — haloperidol is high QTc risk, while quetiapine has moderate QTc risk; dual risk overlap during the cross-taper phase. Anticholinergic cover should be prepared: quetiapine provides no EPS protection, and as it withdraws, haloperidol's EPS risk becomes evident. Consider prophylactic benzhexol once haloperidol is the dominant agent. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start haloperidol 2 mg. Continue quetiapine 400 mg. Baseline ECG before haloperidol. Dual QTc risk during overlap — repeat ECG at day 7–14.
Increase haloperidol to 5 mg (target). Plateau quetiapine — do NOT reduce yet. Assess EPS.
Begin tapering quetiapine to 300 mg. Haloperidol at steady state. Counsel on sleep — H1 withdrawal effect starting.
Reduce quetiapine to 200 mg. EPS from haloperidol should now be apparent — prescribe benzhexol if parkinsonism or akathisia emerging. Quetiapine QTc contribution reducing.
Reduce quetiapine to 100 mg. Sleep hygiene reinforcement. Rebound insomnia may be significant at this antihistaminergic nadir.
Stop quetiapine. Continue haloperidol 5 mg. Recheck QTc. Metabolic improvement expected — document baseline for tracking.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: quetiapine 400 mg ≈ haloperidol 5 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

quetiapine-to-lurasidone.rationale: Quetiapine (high H1, muscarinic, α1 blockade; moderate metabolic risk; moderate QTc) to lurasidone (selective, weight-neutral, low QTc; food-dependent). Common reasons: excessive sedation on quetiapine, weight gain, or metabolic concerns. The quetiapine-to-lurasidone switch is one of the more challenging transitions: quetiapine's heavy anticholinergic and antihistaminergic receptor burden means withdrawal produces significant cholinergic rebound (insomnia, nausea, sweating, agitation). The taper must be gradual and the patient forewarned. Lurasidone food requirement is a critical point of education — must be taken with ≥350 kcal. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start lurasidone 40 mg with main meal. Continue quetiapine 400 mg. Food counselling: lurasidone requires ≥350 kcal for adequate absorption. Warn about likely insomnia as quetiapine is later reduced.
Increase lurasidone to 80 mg with main meal. Plateau quetiapine. Lurasidone approaching therapeutic levels.
Reduce quetiapine to 200 mg. Cholinergic rebound begins — nausea, sweating, sleep disturbance. Do not rush. Melatonin or short-term antihistamine can bridge insomnia.
Reduce quetiapine to 100 mg. Sedation reducing — driving capability should improve. Postural hypotension improving.
Stop quetiapine. Continue lurasidone 80 mg with main meal. Monitor weight and metabolic parameters at 4 and 12 weeks. Improvement expected gradually.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Quetiapine 400 mg ≈ lurasidone 80 mg (inferred from DDD equivalence; both ≈ olanzapine 10 mg by proxy). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

quetiapine-to-olanzapine.rationale: Quetiapine-to-olanzapine switches are uncommon but may occur when quetiapine proves inadequate at maximum tolerated doses or when the antidepressant effect of N-desalkylquetiapine is no longer a differentiator. Olanzapine offers modestly higher D2 occupancy at comparable sedative doses. Plateau cross-taper: introduce olanzapine nocte first, let it reach target, then taper quetiapine; this prevents rebound insomnia and anxiety from quetiapine's pronounced H1/α1 withdrawal. Counsel the patient clearly that metabolic burden increases significantly with olanzapine — this switch does not reduce metabolic risk. Baseline weight and fasting glucose are mandatory before initiating. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start olanzapine 5 mg nocte. Hold quetiapine 400 mg. Both drugs are sedating — advise patient that sedation increases initially.
Increase olanzapine to 10 mg (target dose). Maintain quetiapine 400 mg plateau — do not taper yet.
Begin tapering quetiapine to 300 mg. Olanzapine at steady state, providing full antipsychotic cover.
Reduce quetiapine to 200 mg. Monitor for rebound insomnia as quetiapine antihistaminergic load falls below sedating threshold.
Reduce quetiapine to 100 mg. Sleep hygiene reinforcement. Short-term hypnotic if absolutely necessary.
Stop quetiapine. Continue olanzapine 10 mg. Establish metabolic baseline — weight, fasting glucose, lipids. Schedule 4-week and 12-week metabolic review.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: quetiapine 400 mg ≈ olanzapine 10 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

quetiapine-to-paliperidone-lai.rationale: Oral-to-depot switch in a patient on quetiapine where adherence is the primary concern. Paliperidone palmitate's two-dose deltoid loading protocol (150 mg day 1, 100 mg day 8) achieves therapeutic concentrations without needing a separate oral paliperidone run-in. Oral quetiapine is tapered concurrently with the PP-LAI loading — overlap is safe and provides seamless antipsychotic cover. Key warning: quetiapine withdrawal rebound (insomnia, anxiety via H1/α1) becomes more pronounced as doses fall below 200 mg; counsel the patient and monitor in the final taper phase. Prolactin will rise as paliperidone (high prolactin) replaces quetiapine (low prolactin) — inform before switching. Metabolic monitoring continues — paliperidone's moderate metabolic burden is lower than quetiapine at high doses. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Give Invega Sustenna 150 mg deltoid (loading dose 1). Continue oral quetiapine 400 mg. Counsel patient: 2 loading injections required; maintenance monthly thereafter.
Invega Sustenna 100 mg deltoid (loading dose 2, day 8 ± 2 days). Continue oral quetiapine 400 mg. PP-LAI building toward therapeutic range.
PP-LAI now therapeutic. Begin tapering oral quetiapine to 200 mg. Monitor for H1/α1 rebound at this step — insomnia, restlessness. Sleep hygiene advice.
Stop oral quetiapine. First maintenance Sustenna injection (100 mg; deltoid or gluteal). Monthly thereafter. Check prolactin at 3 months.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: quetiapine 400 mg/day ≈ paliperidone palmitate 100 mg/4 weeks (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

quetiapine-to-risperidone.rationale: Most commonly driven by metabolic concerns (weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia) or insufficient antipsychotic efficacy at tolerated quetiapine doses. Plateau cross-taper: introduce risperidone first and build to therapeutic dose before tapering quetiapine, because quetiapine's abrupt reduction causes rebound insomnia and anxiety via histaminergic/α1-adrenergic withdrawal. The plateau phase gives risperidone time to establish antipsychotic cover. Warning: prolactin will rise as risperidone replaces quetiapine — counsel accordingly. EPS risk increases; monitor for akathisia and rigidity above 4 mg risperidone. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Start risperidone 1 mg. Hold quetiapine 400 mg. Counsel patient about the reason for switch and expected timeline.
Increase risperidone to 2 mg. Continue quetiapine 400 mg (plateau phase — do NOT reduce yet).
Increase risperidone to 3 mg. Begin tapering quetiapine to 300 mg. Cover is now shared.
Risperidone at 4 mg target. Reduce quetiapine to 200 mg. Monitor for EPS as risperidone becomes dominant.
Reduce quetiapine to 100 mg. Rebound insomnia possible at this low antihistaminergic dose — advise sleep hygiene. Short-term hypnotic only if necessary.
Stop quetiapine. Continue risperidone 4 mg. Monitor weight and fasting glucose — metabolic improvement should be tracked.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: quetiapine 400 mg ≈ risperidone 4 mg (Maudsley 15th, AP dose-equivalence table). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

risperidone-lai-to-aripiprazole-lai.rationale: LAI-to-LAI depot switch, most commonly driven by metabolic concerns (weight gain, glycaemic deterioration) or hyperprolactinaemia on risperidone Consta. Aripiprazole LAI (Abilify Maintena) requires a mandatory 14-day oral aripiprazole overlap after the first injection because the depot takes ~2 weeks to reach therapeutic release. Risperidone Consta's residual depot provides D2 cover throughout this oral overlap period. Skip the next scheduled Consta injection when giving the first Maintena. Akathisia is the main switch concern — as aripiprazole's partial agonism replaces risperidone's full D2 antagonism, inner restlessness may emerge. Counsel the patient early. Prolactin will fall substantially as risperidone (high prolactin) is replaced by aripiprazole (prolactin-sparing) — patients with hyperprolactinaemia symptoms should notice improvement within weeks. Metabolic improvement expected progressively. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Skip next Consta injection. Give Abilify Maintena 400 mg IM (gluteal or deltoid). Start oral aripiprazole 10 mg/day — 14-day oral overlap MANDATORY. Risperidone Consta tail provides D2 cover. Counsel on akathisia risk.

STOP oral aripiprazole today (14 days overlap complete). Abilify Maintena now therapeutic. Risperidone depot still fading. Prolactin should be falling — patients notice menstrual or sexual function improvement.
Second Maintena 400 mg injection. Risperidone Consta substantially cleared. Review prolactin, metabolic parameters, akathisia. Monthly Maintena thereafter.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: risperidone Consta 25 mg/2 weeks ≈ aripiprazole LAI 400 mg/4 weeks (Maudsley 15th, LAI equivalence). For Consta 37.5 or 50 mg, consider aripiprazole LAI 400 mg with close monitoring. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

risperidone-lai-to-aripiprazole.rationale: Switching off Consta to oral aripiprazole — typically driven by adherence improvement on aripiprazole-LAI, prolactin/sexual side effects, or patient preference. Skip the next Consta injection; aripiprazole is started early because Consta's depot continues releasing for weeks (effective natural taper). Akathisia is the dominant concern. PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

schedule.notes: Skip the next scheduled Consta injection. Start aripiprazole 5 mg in the morning. Counsel patient about depot tail (Consta continues for ~6 weeks).
Increase aripiprazole to 10 mg. Consta level still significant. Watch for akathisia.
Increase aripiprazole to 15 mg target. Consta level falling but still measurable.
Consta substantially cleared. Aripiprazole 15 mg as monotherapy.

doseRatios.equivalencyNote: Approximate clinical equivalency: Consta 25 mg every 2 weeks ≈ aripiprazole 15 mg/day (Maudsley 14th). PENDING_CLINICAL_REVIEW.

risperidone-lai-to-paliperidone-lai.rationale: Pharmacologically the same molecule (paliperidone is risperidone's active metabolite, 9-OH-risperidone). Switching is primarily for dosing convenience: monthly Sustenna instead of fortnightly Consta.
